items.body:
- [x] I, the PR author, have personally reviewed every line of this PR.

# What does this PR do?

Lets Qwen3.5-VL train on the Mixture-of-Kittens (MoK) MoE megakernel backend from #8210, and makes that path fast. The PR has eight commits, meant to be reviewed one at a time. Commit 1, a router fix for per-layer CUDA graphs, applies to native MoE as well.

## Issue tracking

Linked issue: none. Builds on #8210; commit 6 ports #7391 from `dev`.

## Contribution process

### Pre-checks

- [x] I have added relevant unit tests
- [ ] I have added relevant functional tests (none added; unit tests, bitwise harnesses and a training smoke cover the changes, and gated runs need a newer MoK than the CI image has)
- [x] GPU kernel determinism: the replay test of the changed Triton route-compaction kernel (`mok_route_adapter`) now covers a padding mask; `determinism-exempt` is requested for three other registered files (see Labels)
- [ ] I have added proper typing to my code (new functions are typed, except that `_before_te_cuda_graph_replay`, `_after_te_cuda_graphs_deleted`, `_cuda_graph_megakernel` and `mok_main_grad_arguments` lack return annotations; the `backward` parameter of `_backward_options` and the new `padding_mask` parameter of `RoutingMapToIndices.forward`, whose other parameters are untyped too, have no annotation)
- [x] I have added relevant documentation (MoK section of the MoE README, docstrings)
- [x] Autoformatter: a check-only run of its tools (black, isort, pylint and ruff at the pinned versions) is clean on every commit and on the whole diff

## Summary

#8210 adds MoK as an MoE backend on `main`. Qwen3.5-VL could not use it as is, and the path was slow:

- **Blockers.** MoK failed at step 1 with the Qwen3.5 router settings: router fusion, the Flex dispatcher and HybridEP in indices mode (commit 2). #8210 also rejects Qwen3.5's shared-expert output gate for MoK (commit 6). With per-token loss and no padding mask, capturing the router in a per-layer CUDA graph failed, for native MoE as well (commit 1).
- **Padding.** In the padded Qwen3.5-VL training measured here, about 94% of the routed rows were padding tokens, and the megakernel computed all of them (commits 4 and 7).
- **Host overhead.** #8210 rejects per-layer CUDA graphs that touch the MoE layer for MoK. The router and MoK's per-call host work ran eagerly in every MoE layer and microbatch, and the 397B step was host-bound (commits 3, 5, 7 and 8).

**Headline results.** Qwen3.5-VL training on GB300, MoK against native MoE on the same batch, in the full configuration: this PR with the related PRs below. The qualifiers are under Performance.

| model | at the start of this work | final |
|---|---|---|
| 35B, 8 GPUs, EP4 | -15% to -21% | +39.3% |
| 397B, 64 GPUs, EP32, forced load balancing | +2.9% | +63.8% / +64.7% (two runs, earlier build) |

In a 500-step 35B convergence A/B with two seeds, MoK's mean LM loss over the last 100 steps was within or below the spread of two native variants.

**Related PRs.** The rest of this description uses the short names in bold.

- **MoK PR**, on QiZhangNV/mixture-of-kittens: *perf: routed-row kernels, fused gate backward and eager host path for Qwen3.5-VL* (link to be added)
- **Bridge PR**, on NVIDIA-NeMo/Megatron-Bridge: *feat(model)!: pass a padding mask to Qwen3-VL MoE layers and run the vision merger on graph-padded rows* (link to be added). Its commits 1 and 2 run the Qwen3-VL vision patch merger on the CUDA-graph-padded rows and zero those rows first; its commits 3 and 4 add an opt-in padding mask for Qwen3-VL MoE layers and document it.

## Commits (reading guide)

Each commit builds on the one before it. Commit 1 was first tested on `main`, and commits 2 to 8 each at their own tip on the previous #8210 head. On #8210's latest head, commits 2 to 8 were tested again as a whole, and then all eight commits together, each time against #8210 (see Correctness and validation). Until this PR is retargeted to `pull-request/8210`, its diff also shows #8210, so review only the eight commits on top of `951fd137d`. Throughput and host-time numbers are under Performance. The collapsed blocks hold further details and the unit-test lists.

### 1. fix(moe): count aux-loss tokens on device so moe_router CUDA graphs can capture them

Files: `router.py`.

- **Why.** With `calculate_per_token_loss`, `TopKRouter.attach_and_log_load_balancing_loss` scales the auxiliary loss by the number of local tokens. When that count is a Python `int`, the shape-derived count used when no padding mask is passed, the router built the scalar with `torch.tensor(num_local_tokens, device=...)`. That is a copy from host memory, and a CUDA graph cannot record it. With a padding mask, the count is a tensor, which was already capturable. With the router inside a per-layer Transformer Engine graph (`cuda_graph_modules` containing `moe_router`, or `moe`), capture therefore failed with `Cannot copy between CPU and CUDA tensors during CUDA graph capture`. Qwen3.5-VL 397B training on the native MoE path, with per-token loss, the global auxiliary loss and `[attn, moe_router]`, failed this way at the first graph capture.
- **Change.** The scalar is filled on the device with `torch.full((), num_local_tokens, device=...)`. Its value and dtype (int64) are unchanged, and so is the all-reduce that follows. No other code path changes, and eager execution is unchanged. The `moe_router` and `moe` scopes then work with per-token loss and an integer token count; for MoK, commits 3 and 8 allow those scopes.
- **Evidence.** The new tests capture the router forward with per-token loss in a CUDA graph and replay it; the replay matches eager execution. A 4-layer Qwen3.5-VL 397B training smoke at EP32 on 32 GB200 GPUs with `[attn, moe_router]` and per-token loss captured the router graphs and trained for 20 steps, with native MoE and with MoK. The later full-size 397B MoK runs on 64 GB300 GPUs (EP32) also captured the router with this change.
- **Independent of MoK.** This commit needs neither #8210 nor the other commits, and it also fixes `moe_router` graph capture for native MoE. It can be split out again, to merge on `main` ahead of #8210, if reviewers prefer.

<details><summary>Details of commit 1</summary>

- **Value.** `torch.full((), n)` and `torch.tensor(n)` both produce an int64 scalar equal to `n`. Only the way the scalar is created changes, so no behavior change is expected.
- **Training runs.** They ran on the development tree described under Correctness and validation (main f711d35fe with the #7695 port), with a byte-identical `router.py` change.
- **Unit tests** (`test_routers.py`, new class `TestPerTokenAuxLossCudaGraph`).
  - `test_router_forward_is_capturable[aux_loss|seq_aux_loss|global_aux_loss]` captures the router forward with per-token loss into a CUDA graph and replays it. The replay matches eager execution.
  - `test_integer_token_count_scale_is_captured` captures an integer token count. The test checks that the count is reduced over the group and scales the loss.
  - The class records into a private MoE metrics tracker (an autouse fixture), so its 2-layer aux-loss entries do not leak into the global tracker that later tests read. Without the fixture, `test_aux_loss.py` failed when it ran after these tests in the same process.
- **`dev`.** `dev` has the same code. The `router.py` change applies there unchanged; the test class needs a different insertion point.

</details>

### 2. fix(moe): keep dense routes when a megakernel backend is selected

Files: `router.py`.

- **Why.** With router fusion and the Flex dispatcher, `TopKRouter` asks the fused top-k kernel for compact route indices instead of the dense routing map: int64 for DeepEP and NCCL-EP, and int16 for HybridEP with `moe_hybridep_routing_map_mode='indices'` when the expert count fits. A megakernel backend builds no token dispatcher and consumes the dense `[tokens, experts]` probs/routing_map pair. MoK therefore failed at the first step, in `routing_map_to_mok_inputs`: `probs and routing_map must have the same shape`.
- **Change.** `TopKRouter._dense_route_indices_dtype` returns `None`, meaning dense routes, whenever `moe_megakernel_backend` is set. The check runs before the Flex checks; configurations without a megakernel backend are unchanged. The fused router's compact output then goes unused, which loses nothing, because the megakernel needs the dense pair anyway.
- **Evidence.** `test_dense_route_indices_dtype_keeps_dense_routes_for_megakernel[deepep|ncclep|hybridep]`: each of these configurations compacts its routes without a megakernel backend and keeps them dense with `moe_megakernel_backend='mok'`. No performance effect of its own. All MoK training in this work ran with this change, byte-identical: 35B on 8 GPUs, 397B on 64 GPUs, and the GB200 smoke.

### 3. feat(moe): allow the moe_router CUDA graph scope with the MoK backend

Files: `transformer_config.py`, `moe_layer.py`, `transformer_layer.py`, MoE README.

- **Why.** #8210 rejects every per-layer CUDA graph scope that touches the MoE layer for MoK: `moe`, `moe_router` and `moe_preprocess`. The router, with its gating GEMM, top-k, auxiliary losses and their logging, therefore always ran eagerly, paying its kernel launches and Python on the host in every MoE layer and microbatch.
- **Change.** The router is captured as for the native dispatchers: the layer's TE graph ends after the router and returns its outputs, and the megakernel runs eagerly after the replay, on those outputs. `TransformerConfig` accepts `moe_router` for MoK with `cuda_graph_impl='transformer_engine'`. `moe_preprocess` stays rejected, and so does `moe` until commit 8. With per-token loss and no padding mask, the capture relies on commit 1.
- **Evidence.** A 4-layer Qwen3.5-VL training check ran `[attn, moe_router]` and `[attn]` on the same code: the loss is identical at steps 1 and 2, and later steps differ within MoK's run-to-run variation. All later MoK training used `[attn, moe_router]`, or `[attn, moe]` from commit 8.
- **Known limitations, not changed here:** a stale error text; a `pre_mlp_layernorm` recompute request that is silently dropped with the router graph; `mlp_chunks_for_training > 1`, which fails at capture, as on the native path. See the details.

<details><summary>Details of commit 3</summary>

- **Partial capture.** While the `moe_router` scope is captured, the router raises `MoECudaGraphPartialCaptureSignal`. `MoELayer`'s megakernel branch now catches it and returns the partial-capture outputs, without a shared-expert output, because MoK computes the shared expert inside the megakernel. For megakernel layers, `TransformerLayer` therefore adds no shared-expert graph submodule and pops no shared-expert output from the graph outputs on replay.
- **Config.** The `moe_router` scope is rejected for MoK with the local implementation.
- **README.** The MoK support table lists per-layer TE capture with the `moe_router` scope. In the list of unsupported features, "partial MoE CUDA Graph replay" becomes "the `moe_preprocess` CUDA Graph scope".
- **Training check.** An exact repeat of the `[attn]` run differed from the first run by as much as the two arms differed at later steps.
- **Unit tests** (`test_mok_weights.py`). `test_mok_accepts_transformer_engine_moe_router_cuda_graph` and `test_mok_rejects_local_moe_router_cuda_graph`. The existing reject test now covers `moe` and `moe_preprocess`; it lost its `moe_router`-only cases.
- **Known limitations.**
  - The error raised when a megakernel layer receives intermediate tensors still says "remove moe_router/moe_preprocess". Only `moe_preprocess`, which the config rejects, could lead there now.
  - With MoK and the router graph, a `pre_mlp_layernorm` recompute request is silently dropped.
  - `mlp_chunks_for_training > 1` with a TE `moe_router` graph fails at capture. The native path already fails the same way.

</details>

### 4. feat(moe): give padding tokens no routes in the MoE megakernel path

Files: `moe_utils.py`, `moe_layer.py`.

- **Why.** The router keeps padding tokens in its routes and only excludes them from its statistics. The native dispatchers receive the padding mask and can skip padded rows, as dropless HybridEP does. The megakernel path, however, handed the full routing result to the backend, which dispatched and computed every padding token.
- **Change.** New `moe_utils.drop_padding_routes(routing_probs, routing_map, padding_mask)` returns copies of the dense routing result with the rows of padding tokens zeroed: probs 0 and routing map False. The megakernel path applies it right after `route()` whenever a `padding_mask` is passed. That also covers the unmasked router outputs that a `moe_router` graph replay returns. As with dropless HybridEP, padding tokens then get no routes, and their routed output is zero. Nothing changes unless the caller passes `padding_mask`.
- **Evidence.** In 4-layer training checks, 35B at EP4 and 397B at EP32, native MoE and MoK each had a bit-identical LM loss at steps 1 and 2 with and without the mask. The forward pass of the real tokens therefore did not change; later steps differ slightly.
- **Risk: training semantics.** With a mask, the router's auxiliary-loss statistics exclude padding. The router already does that whenever it receives a mask, but turning the mask on changes training slightly. The mask is opt-in on the caller's side, off by default in the Bridge PR (its commit 3), and model owners should sign off before a recipe enables it by default.

<details><summary>Details of commit 4</summary>

- **Mask layout.** `padding_mask` is batch-first `[bsz, seq]`, with True marking padding. Tokens are flattened sequence-first, as in the hidden states.
- **Placement.** #8210's `route(..., packed_seq_params=...)` call in `megakernel_forward` is kept, and the masking follows it.
- **Cost.** The copies cost one pass over the `[tokens, experts]` probs and routing map per MoE layer, until commit 7 removes them.
- **Unit tests** (`test_moe_layer.py`).
  - `test_megakernel_receives_no_padding_routes[eager|recompute|moe_router_graph_replay]`: the backend receives no routes for padding tokens, and the router call counts match each path.
  - `test_megakernel_moe_router_graph_capture_outputs_unmasked_routes`: a `moe_router` capture returns the unmasked router outputs and does not run the backend.
  - The existing megakernel routing test checks the masked routes. #8210's packed-metadata test in `test_mok_megakernel.py` compares the routes the backend receives by value, because they are now masked copies.

</details>

### 5. perf(moe): cache MoK parameter, main-grad and gradient-sentinel state across calls

Files: `mok/backend.py`, `mok/runtime.py`, `parameter_bridge.py`.

- **Why.** `MoKMegakernel` rebuilt host-side state on every forward and backward: the routed parameter tuples (2 × `num_local_experts` parameters with split expert weights), the main-grad validation and split descriptor tables, and one gradient sentinel per parameter. The autograd function also saved every routed parameter for backward. With many local experts, this host work outweighed the MoE layer's GPU time once padding rows were skipped, so the GPU waited for the host.
- **Change.** The parameter tuples and the sentinel buffers are resolved once. The validated main-grad arguments are cached while every parameter keeps the same `main_grad` object at the same address. `_reset_derived_state()` drops all of this state, and `load_state_dict` and `_apply` call it. Only `x`, the router weights and the shared weights are saved for backward. Each gradient sentinel becomes an alias of one shared buffer per (shape, dtype, device), like Transformer Engine's `get_dummy_wgrad`.
- **Evidence.** In a single-MoE-layer harness on 4 GPUs (GB200), EP4, at Qwen3.5-VL MoE shapes, all 548 gradient tensors are bitwise identical before and after this change.
- **Risks.**
  - **Memory.** The sentinel buffers live for the process lifetime: one uninitialized, parameter-sized buffer per distinct (shape, dtype, device), shared-expert weights included. With single grouped expert weights, that is about one layer's routed and shared expert weights. Before, the sentinel aliased the parameter's own storage. TE's `get_dummy_wgrad` makes the same trade.
  - **Cache validity.** The cache relies on DDP assigning each `main_grad` once. Every call checks the cached arguments by object identity and data pointer, and rebuilds them when either changes.

<details><summary>Details of commit 5</summary>

- **Sentinels.** `param.detach()` allocates nothing, but on a quantized (MXFP8) parameter it builds a tensor subclass in Python, and AccumulateGrad's steal builds a second one. Now `dummy_weight_gradient_buffer` returns one uninitialized buffer per (shape, dtype, device), and `dummy_weight_gradient` returns a fresh detached alias of it. `AccumulateGrad` steals the alias into `.grad` without a copy, also for MXFP8 parameters. All parameters of the same shape share the buffer, and its values are never read. The shared-expert weights get sentinels through `finish_weight_gradient`.
- **Main-grad cache.** The cached arguments include the split descriptor tables. A replaced `main_grad` or moved storage, for example after a grad-buffer offload and reload, rebuilds them, and a missing `main_grad` still raises.
- **Resets.** `_reset_derived_state()` also drops the weight views. In `_apply` it replaces #8210's three invalidation lines; it clears the same state plus the new caches. Commit 8 adds a guard that refuses this reset while a CUDA graph holds the cached views.
- **Saved tensors.** Backward reads the routed weights through the cached views. The routed parameters stay autograd inputs, so each one's `AccumulateGrad` node, and with it the DDP hook, still fires.
- **Unit tests** (`test_mok_megakernel.py`).
  - `AccumulateGrad` steals the sentinel under a DDP-style hook, for a BF16 and an MXFP8 parameter, and no quantized tensor is constructed.
  - The parameter tuples are resolved once, and again after `_apply`.
  - The main-grad arguments are reused until a `main_grad` is replaced, its storage moves or it disappears.
  - The autograd function saves only the backward inputs and still delivers a gradient to every routed parameter.
  - #8210's dtype-conversion (`_apply`) test and the checkpoint test check that every cached field is reset.
  - `test_parameter_bridge_uses_main_grad_and_a_cached_dummy_gradient` replaces `..._without_allocating_dummy_storage`.

</details>

### 6. feat(moe): run the shared-expert output gate inside MoK

Files: `mok/backend.py`, `mok/runtime.py`, `transformer_config.py`, MoE README. Port of #7391 (see Credits).

- **Why.** Qwen3.5 gates the shared expert's output with a learned per-token sigmoid gate (`moe_shared_expert_gate`). #8210 rejects that option for MoK, because the MoK version it pins has no such gate. Qwen3.5 could therefore only run with MoK without the gate, which makes it a different model.
- **Change.** MoK 7a8cfb7 and later apply the gate inside the megakernel, through the `shared_output_gate_weight` arguments of `mok.functional.forward` and `mok.functional.backward`. `MoKMegakernel` registers the shared expert's `gate_weight` as a MoK parameter alias and passes it to MoK, together with its `main_grad` in backward. The gate gradient is finished through the parameter bridge, so its DDP hook fires. `TransformerConfig` no longer rejects `moe_shared_expert_gate` for MoK; shared-expert overlap is still rejected. Ungated layers make the same MoK calls as before.
- **Evidence**, with the real MoK kernels.
  - The ungated path is bitwise equal to the code before this change, at the 35B shape at EP4 and at the 397B shape at EP4 and EP32.
  - On the gated path (35B and 397B shapes, EP4 and EP32), the routed weight gradients and `d_probs` are bitwise equal to the gate-off results, padding rows are exact, and recompute is bitwise. The gate gradient has the same error against an exact reference as native BF16 autograd.
  - 4-layer training smokes, 35B at EP4 and 397B at EP32, tracked native MoE and an MCore-side gate implementation.
- **Risks.** With MoK older than 7a8cfb7, a gated configuration passes config validation and then fails at the first forward call, with a `TypeError` on the gate keyword argument. A follow-up could turn that into a config-time error with a version or signature check, as commit 7 does for its backward option. Gated configurations cannot run in CI yet (see Dependencies).

<details><summary>Details of commit 6</summary>

- **Gate weight.** The alias puts the gate into MoK's parameter-gather hooks; the `shared_experts` module still owns the only checkpoint entry. The gate must be a native, contiguous BF16 `Parameter` of shape `[1, H]`. `_MoKAutograd` passes the gate weight to MoK's forward, and the gate weight and its `main_grad` to MoK's backward.
- **README.** The gate requires MoK 7a8cfb7 or later, which is newer than the MoK snapshot pinned in the CI image.
- **Differences from #7391.** The gate weight is saved for backward next to commit 5's reduced set of saved tensors. #7391's `_apply` hunk is not needed, because `_apply` already resets all derived state (commit 5). The README sentence is new.
- **Unit tests** (`test_mok_megakernel.py`, `test_mok_weights.py`). Gate validation; checkpoint keys with the gate; gate-gradient accumulation into `main_grad` with the DDP hooks, for BF16 and MXFP8 and for split and single grouped weights; a missing gate `main_grad`; and acceptance of MoK configurations with the gate. #8210's checkpoint test keeps its ordered `named_parameters()` assertion for the ungated cases. With the gate, it compares parameter names as a set, because the shared module lists its own gate weight before the parameters of its submodules.
- **Older MoK.** The test group also ran with the MoK a2ad2d0 build in the test container (the commit the CI image pins; it has no gate): the new and re-parametrized tests pass, no test that passes on the parent fails, and the ungated paths are unaffected.

</details>

### 7. perf(moe): fold the padding mask into MoK route compaction and cut per-call host work

Files: `megakernel/backend.py`, `mok/route_adapter.py`, `mok/backend.py`, `mok/runtime.py`, `moe_layer.py`.

- **Why.** After commits 4 to 6, each MoK call still did avoidable host and memory work. It built commit 4's masked copies of the `[tokens, experts]` probs and routing map, and autograd materialized a zero gradient for the integer route indices, which nothing reads. The shared FC1 gate/up views and the main-grad arguments in MoK's six-buffer order were rebuilt on every call, so MoK validated new tensor objects each time. MoK also zeroed the router-weight gradient at unrouted slots, which the route adapter never reads. The 397B configuration was host-bound at this point, so host time per call translated directly into step time.
- **Change.**
  - `MegakernelBackend.forward` takes an optional batch-first `padding_mask`. `MoELayer` passes the mask to the backend instead of calling `drop_padding_routes`, which remains the reference implementation used by the tests.
  - The Triton route-compaction kernel (`RoutingMapToIndices`) drops the routes of padding tokens while it compacts them. Values and the `probs` gradient equal those of `drop_padding_routes` followed by compaction.
  - The indices gradient is no longer materialized, and the views and main-grad arguments are cached. `zero_unrouted_router_grads=False` is passed to `mok.functional.backward` when the installed MoK accepts it; older MoK builds work unchanged.
- **Evidence.** At the MoE-layer level, this commit with the MoK PR's eager host path installed is bitwise identical to the previous commit with the earlier MoK build. The check covers outputs and all gradients, including recompute and step boundaries, on every rank, at the 35B shape and a 397B proxy on 4 GPUs (GB200), and at the real 397B shape at EP32 on 32 GPUs (GB200). With `zero_unrouted_router_grads=False`, filling MoK's router-gradient buffer with NaN before backward changes no result.
- **Risks.**
  - **Interface change.** `padding_mask` is now an optional part of the `MegakernelBackend.forward` interface. Any other megakernel backend must accept it and give padding tokens no routes.
  - **Test-only helper.** From this commit on, `drop_padding_routes` is used only as the reference in tests; its docstring still describes commit 4's direct use. It stays in `moe_utils` as the reference semantics that the new `MegakernelBackend.forward(padding_mask)` contract requires of any other backend, and it can move to the tests if reviewers prefer.
  - **Teardown hang.** One 397B run with these host cuts hung at process teardown after it had finished training. The other 397B runs with them exited cleanly, and the hang was not reproduced.

<details><summary>Details of commit 7</summary>

- **Indices gradient.** `RoutingMapToIndices` calls `ctx.set_materialize_grads(False)` and handles a missing `probs` gradient.
- **Cached arguments.** The shared FC1 gate/up views are valid while the parameter object and its storage address are unchanged. With them and the main-grad arguments cached, MoK receives the same tensor objects on every call and validates them once. The routed FC1 payload is passed directly as both gate and up, as `_gate_up_weight_arguments` already did.
- **Backward option.** Whether the installed `mok.functional.backward` accepts `zero_unrouted_router_grads` is detected once per installed function, from its signature.
- **Unit tests.**
  - `test_multihot_indices_converter.py`: the in-kernel mask matches `drop_padding_routes` followed by compaction in values, indices and `probs` gradient, for boolean, integer and strided masks; the mask is validated; backward creates no zero-filled indices gradient.
  - `test_mok_kernels.py`: the bit-exact replay of the compaction kernel gains a `padded` parameter, which uses a strided padding mask.
  - `test_moe_layer.py`, `test_mok_megakernel.py`: the mask reaches the backend; the cached arguments, views and backward options are covered. #8210's packed-metadata test now asserts that the backend receives `(hidden, probs, routes, padding_mask)`.

</details>

### 8. feat(moe): capture the router and MoK megakernel in per-layer TE CUDA graphs

Files: `transformer_config.py`, `module.py`, `cuda_graphs.py`, `transformer_layer.py`, `megakernel/backend.py`, `mok/backend.py`, MoE README.

- **Why.** With `[attn, moe_router]`, the megakernel still runs eagerly after each graph replay, so its Python host work and kernel launches stay on the critical path of every MoE layer and microbatch. That cost dominates at the 397B shape, which is host-bound.
- **Change.** MoK layers can use `cuda_graph_modules` containing `moe` with `cuda_graph_impl='transformer_engine'`. The layer's graph then covers the router and the megakernel, and its output is the layer output. After warm-up, MoK has static shapes and no host synchronization.
  - **Config.** For MoK, the `moe` scope needs TE 2.19 or later: older TE clones every returned parameter gradient on replay, and MoK returns full-size gradient sentinels. It also needs `pipeline_model_parallel_size=1`. Every validation of the scope ran without pipeline parallelism, where each microbatch's backward runs before the next microbatch replays the layer's graph; pipeline schedules keep several microbatches in flight. The scope is rejected with pipeline parallelism, with `'moe'` in `recompute_modules` and with the local implementation. The `moe_router` scope stays allowed with pipeline parallelism, because MoK runs eagerly after that graph. Megakernel backends do not need the `moe` scope's drop-and-pad requirement, because they have static shapes without it.
  - **Weight views.** A new pre-replay hook refreshes MoK's cached weight views eagerly, including the MXFP8 scale swizzle once per optimizer step. During capture, MoK uses the cached, address-stable views and refuses to reset them while a graph references them.
  - **Warm-up.** TE runs each graphed callable eagerly on its static inputs before capture. All-ones hidden states route every token to the same experts, which can exceed MoK's schedule capacity under real routing. For a graphed megakernel, the static padding mask therefore marks every token as padding, so the warm-up routes none. Replay copies the real mask into the buffer.
  - **Teardown.** Deleting the TE graphs releases MoK's captured weight views, so parameters can be reloaded or moved afterwards.
  - **README.** The MoK CUDA Graph row lists the `moe` scope with its TE, pipeline-parallel and `padding_mask` requirements (see Risks and limitations). #8210's paragraph on per-layer MoK replay now says that it goes through the `moe` scope, which refreshes MoK's weight views before each replay, that whole-layer capture stays unsupported, and that the scope was validated only without pipeline parallelism.
- **Evidence.** In a deterministic harness, the graphed run is bitwise identical to eager in every training tensor, on every rank and step. That holds at the 35B shape and a 397B proxy on 4 GPUs and at the real 397B shape at EP32 on 32 GPUs (GB200), with forced load balancing and with real routing, all without pipeline parallelism. Negative controls: without the eager weight-view refresh, results diverge after the first optimizer step; without the warm-up mask, real routing at EP32 traps in MoK's capture warm-up.

<details><summary>Details of commit 8</summary>

- **Hooks.** The new `GraphableMegatronModule._before_te_cuda_graph_replay` hook runs after the manual parameter all-gather hooks and before the replay. For a graphed megakernel, `TransformerLayer` uses it to call the new `MegakernelBackend.refresh_weight_views()`. `TECudaGraphHelper.delete_cuda_graphs` calls the new `_after_te_cuda_graphs_deleted` hook, which calls `MegakernelBackend.cuda_graphs_deleted()`. The base-class hooks and backend methods are no-ops.
- **Warm-up mask.** Native MoE layers and the `moe_router` scope keep the all-False static mask.
- **Harness.** 2 MoE layers, 3 microbatches and 4 to 5 optimizer steps. Step 1 runs eagerly and the later steps replay the graphs. MXFP8 weights, single grouped expert weights and the padding mask are used, as in production. The checked tensors are layer outputs, input and router gradients, main grads, parameters after the optimizer step, loss and grad norm. Real routing included a case with about 94% padding rows. The logged load-balancing metric is not a training tensor and was not part of the check; it differs in its last bits even between two eager runs of the same configuration.
- **Unit tests.**
  - `test_mok_weights.py`: the TE `moe` scope is accepted (skipped on TE older than 2.19). It is rejected with the local implementation, with MoE recompute, with TE older than 2.19 and with pipeline parallelism, where the `moe_router` scope stays accepted. `moe_preprocess` stays rejected, and the native `moe` scope still requires drop-and-pad. Of the six reject cases of commit 7, four are renamed to `..._covering_moe_preprocess`; the two `[moe]` cases become the TE accept test and the local reject test.
  - `test_moe_layer.py`: a `moe` capture covers the router and the megakernel; the warm-up on static inputs routes no tokens; the static padding mask is all-True only for graphed megakernels.
  - `test_mok_megakernel.py`: weight views refresh outside the graph, BF16 views once and MXFP8 views once per optimizer step. The refresh runs after the manual hooks and before the replay, and only for megakernel layers with the `moe` scope. Deleting the TE graphs releases the captured views.

</details>

## Performance

Qwen3.5-VL training on GB300 with the same batch in both arms, unless a row says otherwise. The numbers in parentheses are commit numbers; the notes below the table use the same keys. Commits 1 and 2 fix failures and have no rows. The full-configuration results are in the headline table, and their qualifiers follow the notes.

| change | setup | result |
|---|---|---|
| `moe_router` graph (3) | 35B, 8 GPUs, EP4. MoK `[attn, moe_router]` against MoK `[attn]` | throughput +5.5% (mean), +5.4% (paired per step) |
| padding mask (4) | 35B, 8 GPUs, EP4. MoK with the mask against MoK without it | throughput +47% |
| | 397B, 64 GPUs, EP32, forced load balancing; same comparison | throughput +26% |
| host-state cache (5) | single-MoE-layer harness, 4 GPUs (GB200), EP4, Qwen3.5-VL MoE shapes, per layer and microbatch | MoK host time, forward + backward: -54%. MoE-layer host time: -46%. Pipelined MoE time: -58% with about 94% of rows without routes; unchanged without padding |
| in-kernel gate (6) | 35B, 8 GPUs, EP4, against the gate applied on the Megatron Core side around an ungated MoK call | throughput +1.6% to +4.4% (four pairings) |
| | per MoE-layer call, harness on GB200: 35B shape at EP4, 397B shape at EP32; same comparison | GPU cost of the gate: about -58% at both shapes |
| mask in route compaction, host cuts (7) | host time per MoE call, 397B shape at EP32 (GB200) | -34% to -37% |
| | 397B, 64 GPUs, EP32, forced load balancing | throughput +12.8% / +13.6% (two runs) |
| | 35B, 8 GPUs, EP4 | about neutral (cross-round comparison; GPU-bound) |
| `moe` graph (8) | 35B, 8 GPUs, EP4. `[attn, moe]` against eager MoE (`[attn, moe_router]`) | throughput +1.0% / +1.4% (two runs; GPU-bound) |
| | 397B, 64 GPUs, EP32, forced load balancing; same comparison | throughput +5.0% (two runs per arm, mean step times; single-run pairings +4.6% to +5.5%). Reserved memory about +10% |

- **(3)** Measured at the start of the work, before commits 4 to 8. Both runs used MoK's default communication and batch settings, with the schedule capacity raised from its default 0.5 to 1.25, and with the shared-expert gate disabled.
- **(4)** Commit 5 was in both arms, the later commits in neither, and the gate was disabled. Each arm ran at its own tuned MoK launch settings, so the rows compare the best settings with and without the mask, not the mask alone; with the mask, fewer communication SMs are optimal. The gain needs commit 5: without its host-side caching, MoK's per-call host work, not the GPU, limits the shorter padded calls. End to end, commit 5 was measured only together with commit 4.
- **(6)** For MoK 7a8cfb7 alone. The MoK PR's fused gate backward lowers the gate's backward cost further.
- **(7)** Measured together with the MoK PR's eager host path. The 397B baseline is the same code without commit 7 and without that host path.
- **(8)** Reserved memory grows because the graph pool keeps MoK's per-layer context. These runs predate the changes listed for the 397B full-configuration runs below.
- **Full configuration** (headline table). The configuration is this PR, the MoK PR, the Bridge PR, tuned MoK backend settings (communication SMs, minibatch and macrobatch sizes, schedule capacity; configuration only) and single grouped expert weights. The native runs use the same padding mask and single grouped expert weights.
  - **35B** ran the final configuration, except for the zeroing guard in commit 2 of the Bridge PR. The guard came later and is bitwise neutral when the padded rows are finite.
  - **397B** ran an earlier build. It did not yet have the Bridge PR's merger commits (1 and 2), commit 8's warm-up and teardown fixes, or the argument and workspace-lookup checks of the MoK PR's eager host path. Each of these changes was verified bitwise neutral; for commit 8's two fixes, that holds under forced load balancing, as used here, and was verified at EP4 and EP32. None of them was re-measured at 397B. The 397B recipe does not set the cuDNN norm flags whose stalls commit 1 of the Bridge PR removes.
  - The 35B full-configuration runs, the convergence A/B and the real-routing bitwise checks used the final pre-rebase code, including commit 8's warm-up and teardown fixes; the GB200 smoke ran this PR's rebased code.
- **Convergence.** A 500-step Qwen3.5-VL 35B A/B with two seeds compared three arms: MoK configured as in the 35B headline runs, native MoE, and native MoE with MoK's MLP weight layout. MoK's LM loss, averaged over the last 100 steps, was within or below the spread of the two native variants: between them on seed 1234, and lower than both on seed 4321. No MoK run in that A/B entered a phase of elevated load-balancing loss.

## Correctness and validation

The bitwise and training checks of each commit are listed with the commit.

- **Measured before the rebase.** The work was developed and measured on main f711d35fe with a port of the same backend, #7695, which is closed and was never merged. It was then rebased onto #8210, which is based on main c919b5e84, and later onto #8210's latest head. #8210 differs from that port only in small fixes: packed-sequence metadata passed to the router, MoE recompute through `precision_aware_checkpoint`, cache invalidation in `_apply`, a removed Transformer Engine API check, a check for missing TE weight storage, documentation and tests. This PR's production code equals the validated code except for three conflict resolutions (two described in the details of commits 4 and 5, and a docstring next to commit 8's capture branch) and commit 8's pipeline-parallel check, which rejects only configurations that were never run. The README text is new. The rebased commits were re-checked with the unit tests and a GB200 training smoke; the throughput runs and the bitwise harnesses were not repeated on them.
- **Unit tests, before the commits were combined.** Commit 1 was tested on `main`, against `main` (GB200): its 4 new tests pass and no other test result changes, on 4 GPUs (`test_routers.py`, where 24 tests that need 8 ranks error at setup on both trees) and on 8 ranks (`test_routers.py` and `test_aux_loss.py`, where everything passes on both trees). On the previous #8210 head, commits 2 to 8 were each tested against their parent on 4 GPUs (GB200): their new, renamed or re-parametrized tests passed (3, 2, 4, 6, 11, 22 and 40 for commits 2 to 8), and no test that passed on the parent failed. On #8210's latest head, commits 2 to 8 were tested together against #8210: no test that passes on #8210 failed, and all 90 new test IDs passed (those 88 and 2 for the pipeline-parallel check). Combining changed no patch: commit 1 and commits 2 to 8 are patch-identical to the versions tested on `main` and on #8210's latest head, so these results still apply.
- **Unit tests, all eight commits** against #8210's latest head (GB200). No test that passes on #8210 fails on this PR, and every new test ID passes:

  | test group | GPUs | this PR, passed / failed | #8210, passed / failed | new test IDs |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | MoE/MoK | 4 | 500 / 44 | 423 / 44 | 94 |
  | MoE/MoK | 8 ranks | 544 / 0 | 467 / 0 | 94 |
  | router | 8 ranks | 224 / 0 | 217 / 0 | 7 |
  | CUDA graph | 4 | 198 / 4 | 198 / 4 | 0 |
  | FP8 CUDA graph | 4 | 5 / 0 | 5 / 0 | 0 |

  The 94 new IDs of the MoE/MoK group are the 90 above and commit 1's 4, and 17 IDs of #8210 are gone (renamed or re-parametrized). The 7 new IDs of the router group are commit 1's 4 and commit 2's 3. The 4-GPU failures are the same tests on both trees and need 8 ranks.
- **Training smoke.** A 4-layer Qwen3.5-VL 35B smoke on GB200 ran all eight commits on #8210's latest head with `[attn, moe]` and with `[attn, moe_router]`. Its tree differs from this PR only in commit 8's comments, README text and one test skip. Both arms completed 30 of 30 steps, and steps 1 and 2 are identical between the arms and to the same smoke before both rebases.
- **Lint.** black, isort, pylint and ruff, at the versions pinned in `pyproject.toml`, are clean for the whole diff of the eight commits against #8210's latest head. They were also clean for every commit against its parent before the commits were combined: commit 1 on `main`, and commits 2 to 8 on the previous #8210 head.

<details><summary>Test groups and other runs</summary>

- **MoE/MoK group.** `test_mok_weights.py`, `test_mok_megakernel.py`, `test_moe_layer.py`, `test_routers.py` and `test_multihot_indices_converter.py` under `tests/unit_tests/transformer/moe/`, and `tests/unit_tests/determinism/kernels/test_mok_kernels.py`. MoK 7a8cfb7 with the MoK PR's changes was first on the Python path. On 4 GPUs, the same 44 tests fail on #8210, at each of commits 2 to 8 and on this PR, because they need 8 ranks.
- **8 ranks (GB200, 2 nodes).** The group, and the router group (`test_routers.py` and `test_aux_loss.py`), pass completely on #8210 and on this PR, including those 44 tests. Apart from the 94 test IDs this PR adds and the 17 it removes (renamed or re-parametrized), the two runs list the same tests.
- **CUDA graph group, commit 8 against commit 7, and this PR against #8210's latest head.** `test_cuda_graphs.py`, `test_transformer_layer.py`, `test_transformer_config.py`, `test_module.py` and `test_vision_cuda_graphs.py`, excluding flaky tests, give identical results; 4 tests need 8 ranks and fail on both. `test_fp8_param.py -k cuda_graph`, which runs TE CUDA graph training loops with FP8 and MXFP8 parameters, passes completely on both.
- **GB200 training smoke.** The Bridge PR's changes were applied. Setup: Qwen3.5-VL 35B with 4 layers on one node (EP4), 30 steps on real data, with the padding mask and single grouped expert weights.
  - Both arms completed 30 of 30 steps without skipped or NaN iterations, and the `moe` graphs captured without a capacity trap.
  - Steps 1 and 2 are identical between the arms in LM loss, MTP loss, load-balancing loss and grad norm. They are also identical to the same smoke before the rebase onto #8210.
  - Later steps differ within MoK's run-to-run variation.

</details>

## Risks and limitations

- **`moe` scope warm-up without a padding mask.** Unless `moe_router_force_load_balancing` is set, the `moe` scope needs a `padding_mask` model input during the eager `cuda_graph_warmup_steps`. The all-True warm-up mask exists only when the layer saw a padding mask during those steps. Without one, which is the usual case in LLM pretraining, TE's warm-up still sends every token to the same experts under real routing. That can exceed MoK's schedule capacity and stop the run with a device-side trap at capture, as in commit 8's negative control. Every validated configuration either passed a padding mask or used forced load balancing.
  - The README's MoK CUDA Graph row states this requirement.
  - Nothing in the code checks it yet. A follow-up should raise or warn at capture when a graphed megakernel layer has seen no padding mask, or give such layers an internal all-padding warm-up mask.
- **`moe` scope and pipeline parallelism.** The `moe` scope is rejected with `pipeline_model_parallel_size > 1`, because every validation of it ran without pipeline parallelism. There, each microbatch's backward runs before the next microbatch replays the layer's graph. With pipeline parallelism, MCore captures one graph per layer and microbatch, which may already keep each in-flight microbatch's MoK state apart, but that is untested. The `moe_router` scope is not affected.
- **Memory.** With the `moe` scope, reserved memory is about 10% higher at 397B, because the graph pool keeps MoK's per-layer context alive. Commit 5's sentinel buffers are covered with that commit.
- **Training stability.**
  - Across the shorter (150-step) 35B runs, MoK runs entered phases of elevated load-balancing loss, some with grad-norm spikes, more often than native runs.
  - That comparison is confounded by initialization. The native recipe uses GLU-interleaved FC1 weights, which MoK does not support, and the native runs with MoK's weight layout also showed the elevated load-balancing loss.
  - The 500-step A/B includes such a layout-matched native arm, and no MoK run there showed such a phase. A larger layout-matched comparison has not been run.
- **Test coverage.** The new tests ran on GB200 only. The MoE/MoK test group ran with MoK 7a8cfb7 and the MoK PR at commits 2 to 8 and on all eight commits together; commits 5 and 6 also ran with the test container's MoK a2ad2d0, the commit the ARM64 (GB200/GB300) CI image pins. In CI, the new tests run only in the H100 buckets: the GB200 unit-test buckets launch only tests marked `launch_on_gb200`, and none of the changed test files carries that marker. The H100 CI images have no MoK. The new MoK tests use fake `mok` modules and Blackwell or TE-version skips, and commit 1's tests need no MoK, so they should pass there, but that is unverified. Watch the H100 unit-test buckets.
- **Per-commit risks** are listed with each commit: the router-scope limitations (3), the training semantics of the mask (4), sentinel memory and cache validity (5), the late failure on older MoK (6), and the backend interface, the test-only helper and a one-off teardown hang (7). Commit 1 changes only how a scalar is created and is not expected to change behavior.

## Dependencies and related PRs

- **Base: #8210**, *Add Mixture-of-Kittens MoE backend on main*, by @FDecaYed. This PR is opened as a draft with base `main` and retargeted to `pull-request/8210`. Merge it after #8210.
- **Transformer Engine 2.19 or later** for the `moe` scope.
- **MoK.** Gated configurations need MoK 7a8cfb7 or later. The MoK PR speeds this path up further:
  - its routed-row processing makes MoK's per-call GPU work scale with routed rows; it is independent of commit 4;
  - its fused gate backward lowers the cost of the gated backward;
  - its eager host path brings commit 7's full host saving and the `zero_unrouted_router_grads` option. Commit 7 also works with older MoK builds.
- **CI image.** The CI image pins MoK a2ad2d0 (`MOK_COMMIT` in `docker/Dockerfile.ci.dev`). Gated configurations cannot run in CI until a separate build change moves that pin to 7a8cfb7 or later.
- **Megatron Bridge.** The padding mask comes from the caller. For Qwen3-VL, commit 3 of the Bridge PR adds an opt-in `return_padding_mask` to the task encoder and passes the mask to the model. The Bridge PR's merger commits (1 and 2) are part of the full configuration.
- The headline numbers depend on the MoK PR and the Bridge PR.

## Labels

- **`determinism-exempt`** is requested.
  - `router.py` (`moe_router`), `moe_layer.py` (`moe_token_dispatchers`) and `moe_utils.py` (`moe_utils`) are registered with the kernel determinism check. Their determinism test, `test_moe_kernels.py`, does not change here, so `tools/check_kernel_determinism_coverage.py` fails on the whole diff without the label, with one issue per file, and passes with it.
  - `router.py` is touched by commits 1 and 2. Neither change, nor the CUDA-graph handling in `MoELayer`, changes numerics; commit 1 creates the same int64 scalar on the device instead of copying it from host memory. The padding masking does change what the megakernel receives for padding rows when a mask is passed. It is a plain `masked_fill` and boolean AND, used only by megakernel layers, and from commit 7 on only as the reference in tests.
  - The changed Triton route-compaction kernel has its own replay test updated (`mok_route_adapter`). `mok/backend.py` and `mok/runtime.py` are registered with an exemption reason.
- **Alternative.** If reviewers prefer a test to the label, a bit-exact replay test of `drop_padding_routes` in `test_moe_kernels.py` would satisfy the check for all three files, because they share that test file.

## Before merge

- [ ] `determinism-exempt` applied, or the `drop_padding_routes` replay test added
- [ ] Retargeted to `pull-request/8210`; CI green, including the H100 unit-test buckets
- [ ] The original author reviews the gate port
- [ ] Model-owner sign-off on the auxiliary-loss statistics with a padding mask, for the Bridge opt-in
- [ ] Links to the related PRs added
- [ ] Follow-ups filed: the CI MoK pin bump, a capture-time guard for the `moe` warm-up without a padding mask, a config-time check for MoK builds without the gate, and a cherry-pick of commit 1 to `dev`

## Credits

- Original in-kernel gate changes by @QiZhangNV in #7391, merged on `dev`. Commit 6 ports them to `main` and carries a `Co-authored-by` trailer for the original author.
- @FDecaYed: commit 2 is two lines plus a comment. It could be folded into #8210 if you prefer.

items.title: [https://nvbugs/6912139][fix] Keep NCCL-EP transport aligned with layer quantization
items.author: nv-lschneider
items.summary: Fix NCCL-EP dispatch inheriting model-wide NVFP4 settings for an unquantized MoE layer. DeepSeek-R1's MTP layer produces BF16 activations, but communication previously rejected them as invalid NVFP4 input: DSR1/GLM-5 MTP layers receive their unquantized config…
items.body:
## Description

Fix NCCL-EP dispatch inheriting model-wide NVFP4 settings for an unquantized MoE layer. DeepSeek-R1's MTP layer produces BF16 activations, but communication previously rejected them as invalid NVFP4 input:

```text
NCCL-EP NVFP4 dispatch requires uint8 tokens with shape (2, 3584), got dtype=torch.bfloat16, shape=(2, 7168)
```

DSR1/GLM-5 MTP layers receive their unquantized configuration through `override_quant_config`. Passing the backend's effective layer configuration to `CommunicationFactory` in `_create_comm_strategy_auto()` is the fix for that path: communication starts with BF16 transport without changing the shared model configuration. Synchronization in `create_weights()` covers a separate case, where `__post_init__` finalizes layerwise/exclusion settings without an explicit override; it is a no-op for the MTP override path.

NCCL-EP reads `QuantConfig.layer_quant_mode`, matching the backend's format interpretation, and stores the resolved transport mode. Unsupported quantized dispatch falls back to BF16 with a warning, so the scheduler dispatches first and quantizes locally afterward. Changing the resolved transport after context allocation remains an error to protect context-owned buffers and descriptors.

The BF16 MTP layer uses a separate NCCL-EP context from NVFP4 layers, including its communicator, EP group, and buffers. Passing effective layer settings to the factory also affects DeepEP/DeepEPLowLatency selection for override models; for example, W4A8_AWQ experts under MIXED_PRECISION can now select post-quant dispatch on DeepEPLowLatency when its other eligibility requirements are met.

This addresses the quantization mismatch exposed during NCCL-GIN regression testing. The GIN context failure was addressed separately in #20146. A common `Communication.set_quant_config()` hook and DeepEP late-finalization support will be handled in a follow-up PR. Forward-porting this release fix to `main` is deferred to the mass merges back to `main`.

## Test Coverage

- Consolidated the original 19 added unit cases into six focused cases: the MTP override through the existing ConfigurableMoE harness; NVFP4-to-BF16 late finalization and context flags; rejection of post-context format changes; and three unsupported-transport fallback cases (FP8/NVFP4 version support and NVFP4 alignment). Existing transport-selection coverage remains intact.
- Review revision: 18 repository transport test cases passed locally using extracted production methods and dependency doubles, plus an additional check that fallback cannot replace an allocated quantized context. These isolated checks do not replace full pytest or GPU testing; local Python lacks pytest and the TensorRT-LLM runtime. Ruff, `git diff --check`, and all commit hooks passed (hooks run with Python 3.13).
- Before this review revision: 145 focused unit tests and six serving runs were reported passing on the PyTorch 26.09 container. Serving covered DeepSeek-R1 FP4 DEP16/MTP1 on GB200 and GB300, and GLM-5 FP4 DEP32/MTP3 on GB300, each with `NCCL_GIN_GPUNETIO_PATH` set and unset. These serving runs have not been rerun for the review revision.
- Serving runs forced NCCL-EP with `NCCL_MNNVL_CLIQUE_ID=$SLURM_NODEID` and `NCCL_MNNVL_CROSS_CLIQUE=0` to exercise communication across synthetic NVLink cliques.
- Removed the waiver for the DeepSeek-R1 FP4 generation-only perf-sanity test. Target selectors:

```text
perf/test_perf_sanity.py::test_e2e[aggr_upload-gen_only_no_context-gb300_deepseek-r1-fp4_8k1k_con4096_ctx1_dep4_gen1_dep16_eplb0_mtp1_ccb-NIXL]

```

items.title: Fix padding-token zeroing for quantized inference under CUDA graphs
items.author: ilml
items.summary: Makes padding-token zeroing in dynamic inference work inside local CUDA graphs. Today it is skipped on every replay, so with FP8/FP4 the padding rows reach the per-tensor amax with whatever stale memory they hold.
items.body:
- [ ] I, the PR author, have personally reviewed every line of this PR.

# What does this PR do?

Makes padding-token zeroing in dynamic inference work inside local CUDA graphs. Today it is skipped on every replay, so with FP8/FP4 the padding rows reach the per-tensor amax with whatever stale memory they hold.

This is why `gpt_dynamic_inference_tp1_pp1_583m_cuda_graphs_fp8_logitsmatch` (GitLab, H100) has failed on every `main` pipeline since 2026-09-17, always with the same output: token 5 diverges from the golden.

## Root cause

#2585 added the zeroing to keep padding tokens out of FP8 amax. It indexes the rows with `inference_context.padding_slice`, a Python `slice(active_token_count, padded_active_token_count)`.

- **Capture:** under local CUDA graphs the slice is evaluated once, at capture. Dummy requests fill the graph exactly at that point, so the slice is empty and the graph records no zeroing.
- **Replay:** a graphed prefill or mixed step replayed with fewer real tokens than the graph holds leaves the padding rows of the attention output unwritten. The varlen kernel only covers the real sequences.
- **Effect:** those rows go through `linear_proj` into the residual stream, and from there into the tensorwise amax of every later FP8 GEMM.
- **Why it only surfaced on 09-17:** before #7093, `--deterministic-mode` NaN-filled uninitialized memory, and TE's amax ignores NaN, which hid the problem. #7093 turned that fill off.

| Site | Captured, so broken, under |
|---|---|
| `attention.py`, `core_attn_out` | layer and block scope |
| `ssm_inference.py`, SSM mixer output `y` | layer and block scope |
| `gpt_model.py`, `decoder_input` | block scope |
| `hybrid_model.py`, `decoder_input` | block scope |

## Fix

`DynamicInferenceContext.zero_padding_tokens(tensor, sequence_parallel_rank=0)` zeroes rows at or past `gpu_view.real_token_count`. That is the fixed-address token count the context publishes on every step, and the MoE routing mask already reads it to mask CUDA-graph padding. All four sites now use it.

The zeroing is a small Triton kernel, `inference/contexts/zero_padding_rows_kernel.py`, following the pattern of `mask_routing_padding`:
- It reads the count on device and stores zeros to padding rows only. It never reads the activation.
- It falls back to `masked_fill_` without Triton or for non-contiguous tensors.

Measured on an A6000 with a hidden size of 4096, per call:

| Case | Kernel | `masked_fill_` | Old slice |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inside a graph, 64 tokens | 1.2 µs | 4.3 µs | — |
| Inside a graph, 512 tokens | 2.4 µs | 10 µs | — |
| Inside a graph, 2048 tokens | 3.3 µs | 54 µs | — |
| Eager, 8192 tokens | 11 µs | 212 µs | 5 µs |

`masked_fill_` rewrites the whole activation. The old slice is not graph-safe.

- **Eager steps:** it zeroes the same rows as before.
- **Steps with no real work** (graph capture, EP dummy steps): the published count is 0, so every row is zeroed. Those outputs are discarded, and the MoE routing mask already treats such rows as padding.
- **Embedding sites under sequence parallelism:** they hold this rank's shard, so they pass the TP rank. Before this change, ranks ≥ 1 left most of their padding rows as `embedding(token 0)` even in eager mode.
- **Hybrid:** now zeroes after its own SP scatter, so both models see a shard at that point.
- **GPT:** skips the zeroing when `decoder_input` is `None`, which is the case on pipeline stages without the embedding. `None[slice] = 0.0` raised `TypeError` there.

Unchanged:
- Models without quantization scales; the gate is not touched.
- MTP draft forwards without the NVLS dispatcher keep the main step's count. The old slice did not cover their padding either.

## Tests

| Test | What it checks |
|---|---|
| `test_dynamic_context.py`: helper tests | Eager zeroing, the SP-rank offset, and a captured CUDA graph replayed with different counts. Capture with 16 or 0 real tokens; stale rows hold finite values or NaN. Each runs on the kernel and on the fallback path |
| `determinism/kernels/test_inference_kernels.py::test_zero_padding_rows_replays` | Bit-exact replay of the new kernel. It is registered in the kernel manifest |
| `TestDynamicContext::test_real_token_count_for_padding_zeroing` | The context publishes 0 on graph capture and the active token count on a graphed step. Called eagerly, the helper zeroes exactly what `padding_slice` covers |
| `test_gdp_dynamic_inference.py::test_decode_ssm_zeroes_padding_rows_on_cuda_graph_replay` | The SSM mixer site under graph replay |
| `test_gpt_model.py::TestGPTDynamicInferencePaddingWithCudaGraphs`, layer and block scope | Captures graphs the way the engine does, replays a 10-token prefill in a 64-token graph with the never-written attention rows poisoned, and checks padding logits are zero |

The quantization gate is patched on so the tests run in BF16 on any GPU.

Checked locally on an RTX A6000:
- On unfixed `main`, the GPT model test (both scopes) and the SSM test fail on their padding assertions. The helper tests fail there because the method doesn't exist yet.
- With this PR, all of them pass.
- `test_dynamic_context.py` shows the same environment-only failures on `main` and here (single GPU).
- black, isort, ruff and pylint are clean, as are `tools/check_process_group_usage.py` and the kernel manifest tests.

Coverage gap: the hybrid embedding site has no CUDA-graph test. It calls the same helper as the GPT site, and with block scope the CLI only allows FP8 as MXFP8, whose per-block scales padding can't affect. The CI image has the Mamba kernels this would need; my local image does not.

Determinism check: `tools/check_kernel_determinism_coverage.py` flags `attention.py`, which is registered as `attention_kernels_and_dispatch`. This PR only swaps the padding-zeroing call there, and the new kernel has its own bit-exact test, so the PR carries the `determinism-exempt` label.

## Expected functional-test impact

`gpt_dynamic_inference_tp1_pp1_583m_cuda_graphs_fp8_logitsmatch` should pass again against its existing golden, with no golden change:
- **Why zero rows match the old NaN rows:** the checkpoint uses RMSNorm and no linear biases, so zeroed padding rows stay exactly zero through the network. That gives the same amax as the NaN rows did before #7093.
- **CI evidence:** in pre-#7093 pipelines, the `..._decode_graphs_only` sibling (eager prefill, so its padding was zeroed) produced tokens and log-probs identical to this test's.
- **Local check:** a small model with emulated tensorwise FP8 used to change by up to 2.4e-2 in log-probs depending on stale memory. With the fix it is bit-identical with and without the NaN fill, and matches the pre-#7093 behaviour.

No other functional test combines dynamic inference, FP8/FP4 and prefill/mixed CUDA graphs, so no other golden should move.

The FP8 test is GitLab-only (`scope: [mr]`), so GitHub CI on this PR does not run it. It needs an internal pipeline to confirm.

# What does this PR do?

Move runtime-service initialization into `initialize_megatron()`, after run-config validation and before distributed/RNG setup.

- Training entrypoints construct/register the config and call `pretrain()`; inference entrypoints call `initialize_megatron()` without separately constructing runtime services.
- Resolve tokenizer-derived vocabulary centrally after tokenizer construction, before writers and other services consume it. Preserve explicit and checkpoint-restored vocabulary.
- Forward `build_tokenizer=False` for heterogeneous MiMo, which supplies its own tokenization.
- Keep the lightweight checkpoint-converter bootstrap, validating its config before creating services.

Most entrypoint changes remove the old explicit runtime/vocabulary calls and their imports. This does not change config ownership, training/inference selection, or distributed/RNG behavior.

This is the separate startup-order follow-up discussed in #7778; #7778 does not depend on it. Pending #7778 and #8149 changes will need to be merged here once they land.

items.title: test: cover eager MFSDP v2 HybridEP cuBLAS corruption
items.author: wujingyue
items.summary: Add a 100-step eager BF16 MFSDP v2 + HybridEP regression for #7400 after the cuBLAS upgrade in #7685. The old library can corrupt gradients while training still exits successfully; the resulting loss divergence fails the existing golden-value comparison.
items.body:
Add a 100-step eager BF16 MFSDP v2 + HybridEP regression for #7400 after the cuBLAS upgrade in #7685. The old library can corrupt gradients while training still exits successfully; the resulting loss divergence fails the existing golden-value comparison.

Preserve the reproducer's GEMM dimensions, EP=2, four optimizer instances, dense/expert outer optimizer sharding, and two accumulation microbatches on eight GPUs. Explicitly select cuBLAS grouped GEMM and NCCL implicit launch ordering. Register one case in the internal GB200 merge-request and nightly suites, using the recipe's default of five repetitions.

Validate all 100 loss samples through the standard CI comparator, using its existing 5% tolerance and allowance for one outlier. The golden file contains only `lm loss`, recorded at full TensorBoard precision.

Validation uses saved NSC LHR training runs on eight GB300 GPUs with the published 26.09-based `mcore_ci_dev` image. Replayed the standard CI pytest comparison after selecting loss-only golden data:

- Shipped cuBLAS 13.8.1.7: all three independent 100-step runs pass, with zero samples outside tolerance and at most 0.55% loss deviation (training job 220207).
- Same image/source/training arguments with only old cuBLAS 13.8.0.4 preloaded: the loss comparison fails on 83 of 100 steps, starting at step 18 (training job 220220). The largest relative difference is 133.26% at step 47: 0.0580261 versus 0.0248759. Final loss is 43.47% higher.
- Four-GPU graph probes, including the existing graph case adapted to mock data, passed on both libraries and did not establish regression detection (jobs 220471 and 220549). The eager reproducer supplies the coverage here.
- Regenerated the selected loss metric from the onboarding TensorBoard events and verified that all 100 values and metadata match the original baseline exactly. Golden-file validation, configuration checks, and `git diff --check` pass. GB200 execution remains for internal CI.

items.title: [hardware, perf, doc] feat: speed up the Qwen3-4B TPU GRPO example by 14% with three overlap settings
items.author: jialei777
items.summary: It changes the defaults of three settings, which are now environment variables: > > > > > > > > Over 100 steps on 2× v6e-4 (4 trainer + 4 rollout chips), the mean step time drops from 25.2–25.6 s to 21.6 s (−14–16%). The 100 steps take 37.7 min instead of 43.3…
items.body:
### What does this PR do?

> This PR tunes the rollout/training overlap of the Qwen3-4B TPU GRPO example ([`examples/tpu/grpo/run_qwen3_4b_torchtitan.sh`](https://github.com/jialei777/verl-upstream/blob/perf/tpu-grpo-4b-overlap-config/examples/tpu/grpo/run_qwen3_4b_torchtitan.sh)). It changes the defaults of three settings, which are now environment variables:
>
> | setting | env var | before | after |
> |---|---|---:|---:|
> | `trainer.v1.separate_async.num_warmup_batches` | `NUM_WARMUP_BATCHES` | 1 | **2** |
> | `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.max_num_batched_tokens` | `MAX_NUM_BATCHED_TOKENS` | 1536 (`MAX_MODEL_LEN`) | **4096** |
> | `actor_rollout_ref.actor.torchtitan.pad_to_length_bucket` | `PAD_TO_LENGTH_BUCKET` | 1024 | **512** |
>
> Over 100 steps on 2× v6e-4 (4 trainer + 4 rollout chips), the mean step time drops from **25.2–25.6 s to 21.6 s (−14–16%)**. The 100 steps take **37.7 min instead of 43.3–44.0 min**, and the final GSM8K validation accuracy is the same (0.953 vs 0.938–0.945). It is a config-only change.
>
> The bottlenecks were found with an RL timeline, built with the timeline tooling from the verl-hardware-plugin branch [`feat/tpu-rl-timeline`](https://github.com/jialei777/verl-hardware-plugin/tree/feat/tpu-rl-timeline) (jialei777/verl-hardware-plugin#9). It draws, per step, what the trainer chips and the rollout chips are doing (figures below).
>
> **Trade-off:** the second queued batch makes training samples staler (about 0.4 weight versions), so the run learns less per step early on. Measured against time instead of steps, reward progress roughly breaks even with the baseline. `NUM_WARMUP_BATCHES=1.5` (or `1`) trades some of the speedup for fresher samples. Details are under *Test*.

Follows up on #8226 (which introduced the 1024-token buckets with micro batch 4) and #8239 (micro batch 2).

### Checklist Before Starting

- [x] Search for similar PRs: https://github.com/verl-project/verl/pulls?q=is%3Apr+tpu+grpo. Related: #8226, #8239, #8243 and #8254. #8254 edits the same README timing line, so I can rebase onto it.
- [x] Format the PR title as `[{modules}] {type}: {description}`

### Test

All runs use Qwen3-4B, GSM8K and GRPO with the script's settings (`TRAIN_BATCH_SIZE=32 ROLLOUT_N=8 MAX_NUM_SEQS=256 MICRO_BATCH_SIZE=2`, validation every 10 steps on 128 samples). They run on 2 single-host v6e-4 slices with `tpu-sync` weight sync, verl `main` and verl-hardware-plugin `e5ab532`. The runs that recorded a timeline used `feat/tpu-rl-timeline`, which only adds the timeline prints; at the time it sat on top of `e5ab532`, and it has since been rebased onto plugin `main` (`f5876f7`).

#### Step time and accuracy, 100 steps

| | baseline (run 1) | baseline (run 2) | **this PR** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `timing_s/step` mean, steps 6–100 | 25.15 s | 25.58 s | **21.57 s** |
| `timing_s/step` median, steps 6–100 | 22.80 s | 22.57 s | **20.09 s** |
| trainer waits for rollout (`timing_s/gen`) | 5.32 s | 5.53 s | 1.54 s |
| 100 steps (sum of `timing_s/step`) / + validation | 43.3 / 47.2 min | 44.0 / 48.1 min | **37.7 / 43.1 min** |
| GSM8K val acc at step 100 | 0.945 | 0.938 | **0.953** |

| steps | 1–10 | 11–20 | 21–30 | 31–40 | 41–50 | 51–60 | 61–70 | 71–80 | 81–90 | 91–100 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| step time, baseline run 1 (s) | 37.2 | 29.7 | 28.0 | 27.1 | 25.4 | 24.0 | 23.1 | 21.9 | 22.7 | 20.9 |
| step time, baseline run 2 (s) | 36.7 | 29.4 | 28.4 | 27.7 | 26.2 | 24.2 | 22.7 | 21.9 | 22.3 | 24.3 |
| step time, this PR (s) | 36.0 | 27.0 | 24.3 | 22.4 | 21.2 | 20.0 | 19.6 | 19.0 | 18.5 | 18.3 |

#### Timeline: baseline vs this PR

Screenshots of the RL timeline report from the verl-hardware-plugin branch [`feat/tpu-rl-timeline`](https://github.com/jialei777/verl-hardware-plugin/tree/feat/tpu-rl-timeline) (jialei777/verl-hardware-plugin#9). To produce one:
- run the job with `VERL_TIMELINE=1 VERL_TIMELINE_RANKS=0` in its environment;
- run `scripts/accelerators/tpu/rl_timeline/make_report.py` on the Ray job log, which writes a single HTML file.

How to read the report:
- The overview rows at the top show what the trainer chips and the rollout chips are doing.
- The "decoding" row shows how many of the 256 vLLM slots are busy.
- The bottom rows have one bar per rollout request. Red bars are requests aborted by a weight sync and resumed afterwards.

| steps | run | step (start → next) | trainer waits | rollout idle | decode slots full | tok/s |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 12–15 | baseline | 32.0 s | 9.7 s | 1.1% | 74.5% | 5.8k |
| | this PR | 27.3 s | 4.0 s | 0% | 93.8% | 6.4k |
| 42–45 | baseline | 26.5 s | 6.6 s | 13.8% | 68.8% | 4.6k |
| | this PR | 20.3 s | 0.9 s | 0% | 91.7% | 6.2k |
| 82–85 | baseline | 23.0 s | 4.1 s | 9.2% | 62.9% | 4.4k |
| | this PR | 18.3 s | 0.0 s | 0% | 83.6% | 5.9k |

**Steps 42–45, baseline.** With one batch queued, each step the rollout finishes its batch and then sits idle (pink "idle"). Meanwhile the trainer waits for the batch's last long responses, and the decoding row decays into a long tail.

![baseline, steps 42-45](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jialei777/verl-upstream/pr-assets-tpu-grpo-4b-overlap/baseline100_steps42-45.png)

**Steps 42–45, this PR.** The second queued batch keeps the decode slots full and the rollout never idles. The trainer barely waits, and every weight sync aborts and resumes the in-flight requests (red bars).

![this PR, steps 42-45](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jialei777/verl-upstream/pr-assets-tpu-grpo-4b-overlap/best100_steps42-45.png)

<details><summary>Steps 12–15 (early) and 82–85 (late: this PR is limited by the trainer, 87% compute), baseline then this PR</summary>

![baseline, steps 12-15](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jialei777/verl-upstream/pr-assets-tpu-grpo-4b-overlap/baseline100_steps12-15.png)
![this PR, steps 12-15](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jialei777/verl-upstream/pr-assets-tpu-grpo-4b-overlap/best100_steps12-15.png)
![baseline, steps 82-85](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jialei777/verl-upstream/pr-assets-tpu-grpo-4b-overlap/baseline100_steps82-85.png)
![this PR, steps 82-85](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jialei777/verl-upstream/pr-assets-tpu-grpo-4b-overlap/best100_steps82-85.png)

</details>

#### What each setting contributes (20-step runs, mean over steps 10–20, no validation)

| run | `timing_s/step` | trainer waits | rollout tok/s | step s per 1k generated tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline | 30.0 s | 7.85 s | 5.74k | 0.175 |
| 2 batches ahead | 28.9 s | 4.8 s | 6.36k | 0.156 |
| 2 batches ahead + 4096 batched tokens | 27.8 s | 3.8 s | 6.44k | 0.154 |

The 512-token buckets only matter once the trainer is the bottleneck, from about step 60. Over 100 steps, they bring the steps 81–100 from 20.2 s to 18.4 s, and `update_actor` costs 3–8% less per trained token.

#### Learning per step vs. per minute

All runs below except the baselines use 4096 batched tokens and 512-token buckets. The reward columns use the 10-step moving average of `critic/score/mean`. "0.90 reached" counts minutes of cumulative step time; the area column averages the reward between 10 and 35 min of step time (higher is better).

| run | `NUM_WARMUP_BATCHES` | mean step | 100 steps | staleness | reward, steps 11–50 / 51–100 | 0.90 reached | reward area, 10–35 min | val acc at step 100 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline (2 runs) | 1 (1536 tok, 1024 buckets) | 25.2–25.6 s | 43.3–44.0 min | 0.90 | 0.853–0.858 / 0.943–0.947 | 21.3–22.1 min | 0.886–0.892 | 0.938–0.945 |
| one batch ahead | 1 | 26.7 s | 45.8 min | 0.83 | 0.860 / 0.943 | 20.4 min | 0.895 | 0.930 |
| 1.5 batches ahead (48 prompts) | 1.5 | 22.4 s | 38.7 min | 1.20 | 0.824 / 0.939 | 20.4 min | 0.882 | 0.945 |
| **this PR** | **2** | **21.6 s** | **37.7 min** | 1.32 | 0.812 / 0.929 | 23.4 min | 0.872 | **0.953** |

- **More batches ahead means faster steps but staler samples and less learning per step.** In reward over time the two roughly cancel; the spread in area is small.
- **With a fixed 100-step budget,** every configuration ends at the same validation accuracy (±0.02 with 128 samples), and 2 or 1.5 batches ahead get there 5–7 min sooner.
- **Fractional values work:** in separate-async mode `data.gen_batch_size` is forced to 1, so `NUM_WARMUP_BATCHES=1.5` queues 48 prompts.

### API and Usage Example

No API change. The three values are environment variables of the script. To get the previous behavior:

```bash
ray job submit --working-dir . --runtime-env-json "$RUNTIME_ENV" -- \
  env RAY_DATA_HOME=/data/<DIR> NUM_WARMUP_BATCHES=1 MAX_NUM_BATCHED_TOKENS=1536 PAD_TO_LENGTH_BUCKET=1024 \
  bash examples/tpu/grpo/run_qwen3_4b_torchtitan.sh
```

To record the timeline, use verl-hardware-plugin `feat/tpu-rl-timeline`:
1. Add `"VERL_TIMELINE": "1", "VERL_TIMELINE_RANKS": "0"` to the `env_vars` of `RUNTIME_ENV`.
2. Build the report: `python3 scripts/accelerators/tpu/rl_timeline/make_report.py --ray-address http://localhost:8265 --job <JOB_ID> -o report.html --summary`.

### Design & Code Changes

| setting | why |
|---|---|
| `NUM_WARMUP_BATCHES=2` | With one batch ahead, a batch is queued only one step before it is consumed, but its 1024-token responses need about 35 s at about 30 tok/s per request. The rollout then idles at batch ends while the trainer waits, steps swing between ~19 s and 27–37 s, and the decode slots average 63–75% full. A second queued batch refills freed slots at once (84–94% full, no rollout idle time). |
| `MAX_NUM_BATCHED_TOKENS=4096` | Every weight sync aborts the in-flight rollouts (about 230 with two batches ahead). They resume as partial rollouts and must re-prefill their prompt plus partial response, about 130k tokens per sync. A larger step budget gets them decoding again within at most 1.9 s instead of 3.0 s, with no change to decode speed. 8192 adds nothing more. |
| `PAD_TO_LENGTH_BUCKET=512` | With `MICRO_BATCH_SIZE=2`, a packed actor micro-batch late in training is about 1,090 tokens, which 1024-token buckets pad to 2,048. 512-token buckets waste less, at the cost of a few extra compiled shapes (about +1.9 s per step in steps 1–10). |

`README.md`: the expected 4B step time changes from "20-30 s (~25 s average)" to "18-27 s (~22 s average over 100 steps)".

**Tried, not included:**
- **512 decode slots:** each request decodes slower, and throughput tops out below 256 full slots.
- **`gpu_memory_utilization=0.85`:** 256 running requests use at most about 40% of the KV cache at 0.6, so it changes nothing.
- **16 `tpu-sync` transfer streams:** the transfer is limited by network bandwidth (~1.1 s either way).
- **`parameter_sync_step=2`:** +6% rollout throughput, but it changes the algorithm.

**Other trade-offs:**
- **Longer validation** (5.4 vs 3.9–4.1 min per 100 steps): validation requests queue behind the extra training batch.
- **Weight-sync pause spikes:** in about a quarter of the syncs, the rollout pause takes 1–7 s instead of 0.1–0.2 s. `vLLMHttpServer.abort_all_requests` waits until every request already handed to vLLM has produced its first token, and some requests are queued behind 256 full slots. Releasing that barrier once a request reaches the engine (as in jialei777/verl-upstream#59) would remove these spikes.

**Noticed along the way, not addressed here** (same in every run, including the baseline):
- **The learning rate never decays.** `TorchTitanEngine.__init__` (`verl/workers/engine/torchtitan/transformer_impl.py`) computes `total_training_steps` but does not pass it to TorchTitan's `TrainingConfig(steps=...)`, so cosine decay runs over TorchTitan's default of 10,000 steps (`actor/lr` is still 1.9996e-6 at step 100).
- **Trainer waits for samples come in 2 s steps.** `ReplayBuffer` waits with `time.sleep(poll_interval=2.0)`, so each waiting step loses about 1 s on average.
- **`actor/grad_norm` spikes to the same values in every run** (about 26.4k, 1,051 and 90). They are clipped by `max_norm=1.0`.

items.title: [https://nvbugs/6511807][fix] Scope NCCL window tensors in the item-scheduled MM encoder step
items.author: pranav-nvidia
items.summary: The engine scopes the LLM forward, the encoder runners, and the MM encoder profiling forward, but not the item-scheduled MM encoder step, which runs before and outside the LLM forward. With tensor parallelism, the vision tower's all-reduces run in that ste…
items.body:
## Description

#17705 requires every NCCL window tensor to be released by its final consumer or by an enclosing lease scope; a window tensor allocated outside any scope that dies through its destructor aborts the process. The engine scopes the LLM forward, the encoder runners, and the MM encoder profiling forward, but not the item-scheduled MM encoder step (`MultimodalItemScheduler.forward_items`), which runs before and outside the LLM forward.

With tensor parallelism, the vision tower's all-reduces run in that step and allocate unscoped window tensors. Mistral Large 3 NVFP4 on 4x GB200 aborts on every rank in `NCCLWindowAllocator::releaseBufferFromDestructor` on the first multimodal request; release/1.3 pre-merge builds 188, 189, 192, 194 and 195 failed this way, and the test was waived in #20259. The same path serves Qwen2-VL and Qwen3-VL.

This wraps the encode step in `discard_nccl_window_tensor_outputs`, matching the profiling forward in `_util.py`. Request state and the encoder cache keep their own copies, made inside the scope, so every window tensor is released when it exits. The test is unwaived.

## Test Coverage

- `tests/unittest/_torch/executor/engine/test_multimodal.py::test_item_encode_runs_inside_nccl_window_tensor_scope` (new): the encode and the cache writes run inside the scope; a full cache hit opens none.
- `accuracy/test_llm_api_pytorch_multimodal.py::TestMistralLarge3_675B::test_nvfp4_4gpus[latency_moe_trtllm]` (unwaived, GB200-4_GPUs-PyTorch-4).

items.title: Stream the same text the non-streaming response returns
items.author: santhnm2
items.summary: The streaming chat path decoded with, which drops every added token flagged. The non-streaming path drops only the tokenizer's special-tokens map and trailing EOS ids.
items.body:
- [x] I, the PR author, have personally reviewed every line of this PR.

# What does this PR do?
The streaming chat path decoded with `DecodeStream(skip_special_tokens=True)`, which drops every added token flagged `special`. The non-streaming path drops only the tokenizer's special-tokens map (`all_special_tokens`) and trailing EOS ids. Chat tokenizers commonly flag their reasoning and tool-call markers as special without putting them in that map (e.g. `<think>`, `</think>`, `<tool_call>`, `</tool_call>`), so in a stream the reasoning parser never saw `</think>`: the answer and the tool-call markup ended up in `reasoning_content` and no tool call was parsed. Thinking-disabled streams and every non-streaming reply were unaffected.

Decode with `skip_special_tokens=False` and drop exactly the ids the non-streaming path drops: `all_special_ids` and the model EOS ids (`model_eos_token_ids`), from both the generated tokens and the prompt prefill. Tokens in the special-tokens map (BOS/EOS/pad) are still dropped.
