items.title: fix: isolate dataset shuffle random state
items.author: LZC-BELIEVER
items.summary: As a result, shuffling the prompt dataset also resets the random stream observed by unrelated code in the same long-lived rollout process, including custom generation or reward functions that use Python's module. This creates hidden coupling between dataset or…
items.body:
## Summary

- Use a dataset-local `random.Random` instance for deterministic prompt shuffling.
- Preserve the existing `seed + epoch` permutation behavior without mutating Python's process-global RNG state.
- Add CPU regression tests for permutation compatibility, reproducibility, and RNG isolation.
- Register the new test in the regular CPU CI matrix.

## Problem

`Dataset.shuffle()` currently reseeds Python's module-level random number generator whenever the dataset changes epoch:

```python
random.seed(self.seed + new_epoch_id)
random.shuffle(permutation)
```

`RolloutDataSource` invokes this method during initialization and at epoch boundaries. As a result, shuffling the prompt dataset also resets the random stream observed by unrelated code in the same long-lived rollout process, including custom generation or reward functions that use Python's `random` module.

This creates hidden coupling between dataset ordering and otherwise independent random operations. Adding or moving a shuffle call can therefore change behavior outside the dataset.

## Fix

Create a dedicated RNG for each deterministic shuffle:

```python
rng = random.Random(self.seed + new_epoch_id)
rng.shuffle(permutation)
```

The local RNG uses the same seed and standard-library shuffle implementation as before, so the dataset permutation remains deterministic for each epoch. Its state is confined to `Dataset.shuffle()`, leaving the process-global RNG unchanged.

No command-line arguments, dataset APIs, sampling parameters, or GPU code paths are changed.

## Testing

The new CPU tests verify that:

- the seeded permutation is preserved;
- `Dataset.shuffle()` does not modify the process-global RNG state;
- independent datasets produce the same permutation for the same seed and epoch.

Relevant CPU regression suite:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. python -m pytest \
  tests/test_dataset_shuffle.py \
  tests/test_filter_long_prompt.py \
  tests/test_read_file_slicing.py \
  tests/test_docs_consistency.py
```

Result: **22 passed**.

Repository checks:

```bash
pre-commit run --files \
  slime/utils/data.py \
  tests/test_dataset_shuffle.py \
  .github/workflows/pr-test.yml.j2 \
  .github/workflows/pr-test.yml \
  --show-diff-on-failure --color=never

git diff --check
```

All pre-commit hooks passed, and `git diff --check` reported no errors.

items.title: [Observability] Add opt-in spans for the colocate offload/onload boundary
items.author: 0z5a
items.summary: This change exposes which operations consume that time: memory-saver pause/resume, memory cleanup, process-group teardown/reload, model switching and diagnostic calls. enables wall-time spans and one summary per call.
items.body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/pull/443/files).

Base: `0z5a-branch` at `791f101e20db377b28e15f12a00863baaea2605f`.

## Purpose

Colocated training currently reports only aggregate `Actor.sleep()` and `Actor.wake_up()` times. This change exposes which operations consume that time: memory-saver pause/resume, memory cleanup, process-group teardown/reload, model switching and diagnostic calls.

`VIME_OFFLOAD_SPANS=1` enables wall-time spans and one summary per call. The default path skips the extra clock reads and emits nothing. Nested spans retain inclusive child/parent totals, while `accounted_s` counts root intervals once. Training, tensor transfers and returned values retain their existing behavior.

The submitted diff contains two production files. Test harnesses, logs and their added CI registration were removed; their measured results are retained below.

## Validation

- **8 CPU tests pass:** disabled-path clock/log behavior, repeated spans, nested accounting, dotted sibling names, exception unwinding, reset, rounding and output ordering.
- RTX 5090 Qwen3-0.6B full training smokes cover vLLM rollout, reference/actor forwards, backward and optimizer, checkpoint saving and weight publication.
- Three independent paired six-round runs compare the previous accounting implementation with this revision. Each arm starts in a fresh process; round zero is excluded. An additional enabled-span training round verifies the emitted ledger.
- The implementation revision passed Buildkite [#1323](https://buildkite.com/vllm/vime-ci/builds/1323), DCO and documentation checks before artifact cleanup. The cleanup leaves production code byte-for-byte unchanged; its new head receives the normal automatic checks.

## Measured results

Default-disabled spans, Qwen3-0.6B, two prompts × two samples, 16 response tokens maximum. Driver round time includes rollout, training, offload and weight publication.

| Pair / order | Parent median round (s) | Candidate median round (s) | Observed ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 / parent → candidate | 10.761 | 9.782 | 1.100× |
| 2 / candidate → parent | 11.836 | 11.300 | 1.047× |
| 3 / parent → candidate | 11.563 | 11.516 | 1.004× |
| Median paired ratio | | | 1.047× |

Generated response lengths vary between arms. These timings do not establish a causal training speedup from the accounting change. The CPU microbenchmark observes approximately 1.1 μs per disabled context-manager invocation; enabled nested accounting costs about 2% more than its previous implementation.

With spans enabled in a separate diagnostic round:

| Call | Total (s) | Accounted (s) | Residual (s) | Largest segment |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `sleep` | 1.435661 | 1.435575 | 0.000087 | TMS pause: 1.133446 s |
| `wake_up` | 1.029749 | 1.029621 | 0.000128 | TMS resume: 0.617490 s |

A separate existing `--no-offload-train` configuration comparison observed a 4.345× median ratio. That result is not caused by the span patch. Multi-rank coverage remains outstanding.

items.title: [RFC] Colocate offload/onload dominates step time on small-model short-response workloads
items.author: 0z5a
items.summary: This closes out the roadmap item in #11: > Residual rollout overhead profiling (py-spy RolloutManager) — the remaining ~3-4% gap after router + logprobs fixes is in framework overhead, not engine/router The residual is not in framework overhead. Measured end-t…
items.body:
## Summary

This closes out the roadmap item in #11:

> Residual rollout overhead profiling (py-spy RolloutManager) — the remaining ~3-4% gap after router + logprobs fixes is in framework overhead, not engine/router

**The residual is not in `RolloutManager` framework overhead.** Measured end-to-end on the baseline, the whole post-rollout framework path (`convert_samples` + `split_by_dp` + `log_rollout_data`) is **13.5 ms/step at N=16 and 124.9 ms/step at N=256 — 0.08% / 0.18% of the step**, and the `RolloutManager` process is ~98% idle in CPU terms.

What *does* dominate the serial part of a colocate step on this workload is the **Megatron offload/onload dance**: `Actor.sleep()` + `Actor.wake_up()` (i.e. `torch_memory_saver.pause()/resume()` plus `destroy_process_groups()`/`reload_process_groups()`) costs **11.27 s/step, 66.9% of the step at N=16** and 8.32 s/step (12.2%) at N=256. In colocate mode this defaults on: `offload_train is None → True` in `vime/utils/arguments.py`.

This issue tracks that as its own work item. The profiling side is already delivered; no optimization PR exists yet because the measured target turned out to be a different subsystem than the roadmap assumed.

## Measurement

1× L20 colocate, Qwen3-0.6B dense, GRPO, dapo-math-17k, `--rollout-max-response-len 192`, `--vllm-gpu-memory-utilization 0.4`, 8 rollouts. Steady state only (first cycles dropped). Baseline SHA `791f101e20db377b28e15f12a00863baaea2605f`.

### Where a colocate step goes

| stage | N=16 | % of step | N=256 (canonical) | % of step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `perf/step_time` (= train_wait + train) | 16.848 s | 100.00% | 68.061 s | 100.00% |
| `perf/train_wait_time` | 12.841 s | 76.22% | 16.122 s | 23.69% |
| `perf/train_time` | 3.992 s | 23.69% | 51.939 s | 76.31% |
| ├ `perf/actor_train_time` | 2.962 s | 17.58% | 43.524 s | 63.95% |
| ├ `perf/ref_log_probs_time` | 0.656 s | 3.89% | — | — |
| └ `perf/update_weights_time` | 0.376 s | 2.23% | — | — |
| **`perf/sleep_time`** (offload) | **7.748 s** | **45.99%** | — | — |
| **`perf/wake_up_time`** (onload) | **3.147 s** | **18.68%** | — | — |
| `perf/sleep_time` + `perf/wake_up_time` | **10.895 s** | **64.67%** | 8.321 s | **12.23%** |
| `perf/data_preprocess_time` | 0.0047 s | 0.03% | 0.0634 s | 0.09% |

### The subsystem that was suspected — and is not the problem

| post-rollout span | N=16 | % of step | N=256 | % of step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `manager.convert_samples` | 0.693 ms | 0.0041% | 3.60 ms | 0.0053% |
| `manager.split_by_dp` | 13.330 ms | 0.0791% | 113.58 ms | 0.1669% |
| ├ `split.package_ranks` (`ray_put` / `tensorize`) | 13.118 ms (9.322 / 2.844) | 0.0779% | 111.06 ms (74.62 / 36.22) | 0.1632% |
| └ `split.build_dp_schedule` | 0.060 ms | 0.0004% | 0.40 ms | 0.0006% |
| `manager.log_rollout_data` | 1.908 ms | 0.0113% | 7.72 ms | 0.0113% |
| **post-rollout framework total** | **13.52 ms** | **0.080%** | **124.90 ms** | **0.184%** |

Scaling samples 16× grows this path ~9.2×, but its share of the step only moves from 0.08% to 0.18% — still more than an order of magnitude below the 3–4% the roadmap item assumed, and the largest single item (`split.ray_put`, 74.6 ms at N=256) is 0.11% of the step.

py-spy on the `RolloutManager` actor (`--format speedscope --nonblocking --rate 100 --duration 150`): **2.59 s of CPU over the whole window**; the top frames are the interpreter `<module>` (0.69 s) and Ray's own `main_loop` (0.67 s); the only VIME frame that registers at all is `_cpu_tensor` (self 0.02 s). The actor is ~98% blocked on the vLLM HTTP response, so there is no CPU hotspot to remove.

### Candidate optimizations that were falsified

Rather than stopping at "the share is small", each plausible framework candidate was measured both ways (CPU microbenchmark and live spans), and they agree, which is what makes the negative result credible:

| candidate | microbenchmark | live span | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[sum(m) for m in loss_masks]` + mask construction | 0.113 ms @N=256; 0.77 ms at 395k tokens | `convert.loss_masks` 0.011 ms, `convert.rollout_mask_sums` 0.052 ms | falsified |
| `calculate_fwd_flops` (2N single-element calls) | whole-batch vs per-element only 1.32×, 0.152 ms | `split.build_dp_schedule` 0.060 ms | falsified |
| per-rank packing list comprehensions | 0.031 ms @N=256 | `split.package_ranks` 13.1 ms, of which pure Python <1 ms | falsified |
| `log_rollout_data` metric aggregation | 2.53 ms @N=256 | 1.908 ms | predicted ≈ measured, but harmless in absolute terms |
| `tensorize_rollout_data_for_training` | 3.09 ms @N=256 | 2.844 ms | predicted ≈ measured, but harmless |

## Why this is worth a separate item

`Actor.sleep()` and `Actor.wake_up()` sit on the critical path of every colocate step and are pure overhead from the RL algorithm's point of view — GPU work that exists only to make room for the other engine. At 65% of a small-model step, this is the largest single lever measured so far, and it is invisible in the rollout-side metrics that the roadmap item was looking at, because it is charged to `perf/train_wait_time`.

The concrete questions worth answering:

1. **Break down the 11.27 s.** It is `clear_memory(clear_host_memory=True)` + `destroy_process_groups()` + `torch_memory_saver.pause()` on the way down, and `resume()` + `clear_memory()` + `reload_process_groups()` (+ a WORLD barrier when PP>2) on the way up. Which of those actually costs the seconds is not measured yet — this is the first thing to profile, and it decides whether the fix is an offload-policy change or a process-group-lifetime change.
2. **Is per-step offload necessary at all** for a given memory budget? `--release-train` already exists as an alternative that releases the Megatron actors instead of memory-saver pausing them; and `offload_train` can be turned off explicitly. Neither has been compared against the default on a real workload.
3. **Can the dance overlap the rollout?** During rollout the trainer is idle by construction; today it offloads and waits, then onloads after. Whether the onload can start earlier (or the offload be made incremental) is open.

## Non-goals

- Not proposing to change `RolloutManager`. That path is measured and is not worth touching at this scale.
- Not proposing a change to weight-transfer semantics. Nothing here touches NCCL/weight-update correctness.

## Acceptance for the follow-up

Paired A/B on the same workload and the same node, ≥5 steady-state cycles, reporting `perf/step_time` delta together with the observed run-to-run spread — this is a shared node and the same span was seen to vary by up to an order of magnitude within one window, so a single arm is not evidence.

## Limitations

- Single L20, 1-GPU colocate, Qwen3-0.6B, short responses (cap 192). Longer responses, larger models, TP/DP>1 and non-colocate are not covered; the balance between `sleep/wake` and `actor_train_time` clearly shifts with model size (it already flips between the two columns above), so the 65% figure should not be generalized.
- The `sleep`/`wake_up` timers are VIME's own and were not independently cross-validated in this round.
- `train_wait_time ≈ sleep + wake_up + rollout + scheduling slack` is a magnitude-level consistency check, not an independently measured decomposition; those timers may overlap and were deliberately not subtracted.
- Measured on a shared node (load 52–137 during the timing windows); reported values are medians, not a noise floor.

## Reproduction

```bash
# container: L20 needs TransformerEngine rebuilt for sm_89
scripts/recreate.sh

# E2E with opt-in post-rollout spans + py-spy
scripts/prof.sh

# CPU-side cross-checks
python3 bench_a4_cpu.py     --src /work/vime --repeats 5 --json out1.json
python3 bench_a4_parts.py   --src /work/vime --json out2.json
python3 bench_a4_metrics.py --src /work/vime --repeats 5 --json out3.json
```

The spans used for the tables above are opt-in and off by default (`VIME_A4_SPANS=1`); they are proposed for main in #437.
discussion:
Item 1 from the issue — what the 11.27 s is actually made of — is measured. Instrumentation and numbers are in #443.

## Setup

1 GPU colocate, Qwen3-0.6B, GRPO, `rollout_batch_size 8 x n_samples 2`, cap 192, 8 rollouts, steady state (first call dropped). Segments are medians of the per-call spans.

| stage | median | share of step |
|---|---|---|
| `perf/step_time` | 18.853 s | 100.0% |
| `perf/train_wait_time` | 17.425 s | 92.4% |
| `perf/train_time` | 0.864 s | 4.6% |
| **`perf/sleep_time`** | **11.228 s** | **59.6%** |
| **`perf/wake_up_time`** | **3.773 s** | **20.0%** |
| **sleep + wake_up** | **15.000 s** | **79.6%** |
| `perf/update_weights_time` | 0.534 s | 2.8% |
| `perf/data_preprocess_time` | 0.005 s | 0.0% |

(The share is higher than the 66.9% in the issue because rollout was cheaper in this window — 1.3 s. The absolute sleep/wake numbers are in the same range as before, a little worse, on a node at load ~14.)

## `sleep()` — median 11158 ms

| segment | median | share |
|---|---|---|
| **`torch_memory_saver.pause()`** | **9680.5 ms** | **86.8%** |
| `destroy_process_groups()` | 914.1 ms | 8.2% |
| `clear_memory(clear_host_memory=True)` | 441.6 ms | 4.0% |
| `print_memory()` (two calls) | 2.2 ms | 0.0% |

## `wake_up()` — median 3772 ms

| segment | median | share |
|---|---|---|
| **`torch_memory_saver.resume()`** | **3172.6 ms** | **84.1%** |
| `clear_memory()` | 492.7 ms | 13.1% |
| `_switch_model("actor")` | 107.0 ms | 2.8% |
| `reload_process_groups()` | 8.3 ms | 0.2% |
| `print_memory()` (two calls) | 3.0 ms | 0.1% |

The segments are disjoint and account for 100.0% of both calls, so nothing is hiding between them.

## What this decides

**The answer to "which of those actually costs the seconds" is the memory-saver transfer**: 9680 + 3173 = 12.85 s of the 14.93 s measured across the two calls, 86%.

That rules out both alternatives the issue listed as live options:

* **Process-group lifetime is not it.** `destroy_process_groups()` + `reload_process_groups()` = 922 ms, 6% combined. Worth dropping from consideration.
* `clear_memory()` is 934 ms combined (6%) — second order, and `_host_emptyCache()` is inside it.
* `print_memory()` costs ~5 ms across both calls despite being called four times per step.

## The transfer has an order of magnitude of headroom

From the same run's memory samples:

| | volume | time | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pause()` frees | 18.71 GB | 11.228 s | **1.67 GB/s** |
| `resume()` restores | 17.21 GB | 3.773 s | **4.56 GB/s** |

The link is PCIe Gen4 x16, and neither direction comes close to it. Two details worth keeping in mind for whoever picks this up:

* ~18.7 GB is parked, not the 1.2 GB of bf16 weights: the fp32 master weights, Adam moments and gradients dominate the footprint. Shrinking what has to move is as viable as moving it faster.
* `resume()` is 2.7x faster than `pause()` for the same volume, which suggests `pause()` is doing more than copying.

So of the three directions in the issue, (1) is now closed and it points at the transfer; (2) `--release-train` is still open but is a different trade (it releases the actors instead of parking them) and only matters if the transfer cannot be fixed; (3) overlapping with rollout is worth revisiting once the transfer cost is known, since the trainer is idle for only ~1.3 s of an 11 s offload here.

Follow-up on the breakdown above: the transfer's headroom is now measured, and it is not in this repository.

## The machine is not the limit

Same GPU, same 4 GiB volume, with `LD_PRELOAD` and the `TMS_INIT_ENABLE*` variables set exactly as `vime/ray/actor_group.py` sets them for the actor processes:

| path | D2H | H2D |
|---|---|---|
| torch, pinned host buffer | 24.43 GiB/s | 23.54 GiB/s |
| torch, pageable host buffer | 8.75 GiB/s | 9.01 GiB/s |
| **`torch_memory_saver`** | **2.41 GiB/s** | **5.32 GiB/s** |

`nvidia-smi` reports the link trained to Gen4 x16 while these run. TMS is an order of magnitude below a plain pinned `copy_()` and 3.6x below even a pageable one.

## It is the copy, not the allocator work

Same pause/resume with `TMS_INIT_ENABLE_CPU_BACKUP=0` (drop the memory, keep no copy):

| size | pause, backup on | pause, backup off |
|---|---|---|
| 1 GiB | 424 ms | 2.0 ms |
| 2 GiB | 1231 ms | 4.8 ms |
| 4 GiB | 2842 ms | 7.7 ms |
| 8 GiB | 5992 ms | 30.0 ms |

VMM/allocator/free work is a few ms per GiB; the rest is the CPU-backup `cudaMemcpy`. (The backup-on column accumulates earlier iterations' cached blocks so it runs slightly high; a clean single-tensor repeat of 4 GiB gives 1658 ms.)

## TMS's other modes are worse

| mode, 4 GiB | pause | resume |
|---|---|---|
| CPU backup | 1658 ms | 752 ms |
| disk backup | 49766 ms | 21052 ms |
| no backup (contents lost) | 7.7 ms | 6.0 ms |

So the mode VIME already uses is the fastest of the three.

## What this means for the items in the issue

* **Item 1 is closed and it points outside this repository.** The seconds are inside `torch_memory_saver`'s copy path (0.0.9.post1+slime here; whether a newer release improves it was not tested). A change in VIME cannot move that rate.
* **Item 2 (`--release-train`) becomes the main VIME-side lever**, because the only thing this repository controls is *how much is parked*: ~18.7 GB for a 0.6B model, dominated by fp32 master weights, Adam moments and gradients. That is also the direction the "offload optimizer state to host RAM" pattern takes.
* **Item 3 (overlap) is not attractive as measured**: the trainer is idle for only ~1.3 s of an 11 s offload, so there is nothing to hide the copy behind on this workload.

Method and raw numbers are in #443.

Item 2 of the issue — not parking at all — now has a number, and it is the largest one so far.

`--offload-train` defaults to true under `--colocate`, but it is not forced by it: `utils/arguments.py` only sets it when it is unset, and an explicit `--no-offload-train` is honoured. Same 1 GPU colocate workload, same vLLM memory budget, same tree, 7 steady rollouts each, everything else identical:

| | offload on (default) | `--no-offload-train` |
|---|---|---|
| `perf/step_time` | 18.853 s | **3.316 s** |
| `perf/sleep_time` | 11.228 s | — |
| `perf/wake_up_time` | 3.773 s | — |
| `perf/train_wait_time` | 17.425 s | 2.486 s |
| `perf/train_time` | 0.864 s | 0.815 s |
| `perf/update_weights_time` | 0.534 s | 0.347 s |

**5.7x on the step**, and it lines up exactly with the breakdown above: what disappears is `sleep()` + `wake_up()` (15.0 s of 18.9 s) and nothing else moves. `train_time` is unchanged at ~0.8 s.

The catch is memory. The training state (~20 GB here, and the copy moves ~18.7 GB of it) and the rollout engines have to be resident at the same time, so the vLLM budget has to leave room for it. At 0.6B that fits comfortably on a 44 GB card; at a scale where it does not, the offload is not optional and the current default is the only option.

Two things follow from this that want a decision rather than a patch:

1. **The help text is wrong and points away from this.** It says the flag "will always be true when `--colocate` is set", which is not what the code does. Corrected in #445.
2. **Should VIME choose this automatically?** Deriving it from free memory at startup is plausible, but a wrong guess turns into a rollout-engine OOM during init, so I left the default alone. Worth deciding deliberately — and the failure mode is at least loud and immediate rather than silent.

For reference, the intervening attempts to measure this are also a small lesson in shared-node work: four runs were defeated before this one by other tenants taking the device mid-startup (two of them arriving between the moment a GPU was chosen and the moment vLLM requested its memory), which shows up as `cumem_allocator.cpp` OOM inside vLLM's sleep-mode `wake_up`, not as an OOM in our own code.

items.title: [Bugfix][Rollout] Report engine drain state after an abort
items.author: 0z5a
items.summary: Observe actual engine drain after request abortion. An abort response or empty local pending set does not establish server idleness: late requests and unreadable engine state are reported as busy or unknown.
items.body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/pull/440/files).

Base: `0z5a-branch` at `791f101e20db377b28e15f12a00863baaea2605f`.

Observe actual engine drain after request abortion. An abort response or empty local pending set does not establish server idleness: late requests and unreadable engine state are reported as busy or unknown.

Probe per-rank metrics, queue counts and `num_requests` in order, using deadline-bounded parallel requests and a bounded late-request resweep. The result is logged; this change does not enforce a new fail-closed weight-update policy.

| Validation | Before | Candidate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU drain checks | 8 failed, 22 passed | 30 passed |
| Live engine: 12 requests then abort | 12 active | 0 active |
| Request arriving after the sweep | — | 1 active; drain reported false |
| Second sweep | — | 0 active; drain reported true |
| Qwen3-0.6B GRPO, 2×L20, 5 rollouts | — | All five confirmed drained |

| Rollout | Drain probe latency | Confirmed idle |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| 0 / 1 / 2 | 41 ms each | Yes |
| 3 / 4 | 46 ms each | Yes |

The model run oversampled 24 requests and exercised rollout, training and weight publication. Probe latency is added diagnostic work, not a speedup. Added tests and their CI registration were removed from the diff.

items.title: [Bugfix][Rollout] Preserve per-request transfer metrics through MultiConnector
items.author: 0z5a
items.summary: Preserve per-request transfer metrics when wraps. Its worker metadata previously dropped the child's request statistics before scheduler aggregation.
items.body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/pull/439/files).

Base: `0z5a-branch` at `791f101e20db377b28e15f12a00863baaea2605f`.

Preserve per-request transfer metrics when `MultiConnector` wraps `NixlConnector`. Its worker metadata previously dropped the child's request statistics before scheduler aggregation.

Add the merge to the existing Docker vLLM patch: combine distinct requests and fields, sum matching counters, skip absent child metrics and rebuild each read without mutating child metadata. No new test files are submitted.

| Real-class validation in built `vllm/vime:latest` | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Before the added patch hunk | 8 failed, 2 passed |
| Patch application | Passed |
| After the hunk | 10 passed |

Single-L20 prefill/decode experiment:

| Connector | Remote KV wait (ms) | Transfer bytes | Worker transfer (ms) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Direct Nixl | 63.85 | 1,835,008 | 24.34 |
| Wrapped Nixl, unpatched | 433.52 | Missing | Missing |
| Wrapped Nixl, patched | 630.23 | 1,835,008 | 581.81 |

The recovered byte count establishes propagation. These single runs do not establish latency improvement. CI uses a prebuilt image and does not rebuild this Docker patch; the patched-runtime checks above were run separately.

items.title: feat: add backend-aware SUPA (Biren) support
items.author: kakyo82
items.summary: Following the backend-aware MUSA support merged in #2216, this PR registers a SUPA accelerator backend for Biren GPUs through the same abstraction. It adds no new abstraction and changes no shared behavior — SUPA is simply a second vendor plugged into the regi…
items.body:
## Motivation

Following the backend-aware MUSA support merged in #2216, this PR registers a
**SUPA** accelerator backend for Biren GPUs through the same
`slime.utils.accelerator` abstraction. It adds no new abstraction and changes
no shared behavior — SUPA is simply a second vendor plugged into the registry
that #2216 already established (ABC → `TorchAccelerator` → vendor subclass).

## Modifications

- **`slime/utils/accelerator/supa.py`** (new): `SUPAAccelerator`, a
  `TorchAccelerator` subclass delegating to the `torch.supa` namespace. It declares:
  - `bccl` as the communication backend;
  - `SUPA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` as the visibility env;
  - `"cpu:gloo,supa:bccl"` as the weight-update backend (the Biren runtime
    accepts both the plain `bccl` and the device-qualified `supa:bccl` form);
  - a no-op `distributed_device_id` so the SUPA runtime binds the device itself.

  It never imports the vendor runtime at module import time.
- **`slime/utils/accelerator/__init__.py`**: register `"supa"` (priority 150,
  `communication_backends=("bccl",)`) and add a bootstrap chain that loads the
  SUPA runtime only after SUPA has won backend selection — a CUDA or CPU-only
  host never touches it (mirrors the MUSA `musa_patch` bootstrap).
- **`slime/ray/utils.py`**: honor `RAY_EXPERIMENTAL_NOSET_SUPA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`,
  matching the existing CUDA / MUSA entries.
- **`tests/test_accelerator.py`**: 5 new tests covering SUPA selection, one-shot
  bootstrap, device / process-group mapping, `bccl` backend recognition, and
  graceful handling of a missing `torch.supa` namespace.

## Verification

- All new tests run with `num_gpus: 0` and require **no Biren hardware** — they
  use monkeypatched availability and a fake `torch.supa`, exactly like the
  existing MUSA tests.
- `pytest tests/test_accelerator.py` → **14 passed** on a CPU-only
  `torch==2.10.0+cpu` host.
- The change is **purely additive**: no existing CUDA or MUSA code path is
  modified. `test_cuda_selection_does_not_bootstrap_supa` guards that a CUDA
  host never loads the SUPA runtime.

## Checklist

- [x] New backend is opt-in and does not alter CUDA/MUSA behavior.
- [x] Tests pass in CI without vendor hardware (`num_gpus: 0`).
- [x] Follows the structure of the merged MUSA backend (#2216).
discussion:
Hi @zhuzilin 
I’ve opened this PR to adapt Slime for Biren GPUs based on the backend-aware structure from  #2216 . The changes register a  supa  accelerator backend in a purely additive way, ensuring zero impact on existing CUDA/MUSA paths.
All new tests are CI-verifiable without Biren hardware (using mocked  torch.supa , mirroring the MUSA tests).
Could you please take a look when you have a chance? Happy to provide any additional tests or experimental results if needed. Thanks!

items.title: [RFC]  Support DSpark on Ascend NPU
items.author: miracle0517
items.summary: This RFC proposes enabling DSpark speculative decoding support on Ascend NPU within the Vime framework. The change adapts the NPU batch-reordering logic to accommodate DSpark's speculative-decoding layout requirements, allowing DSpark to be launched alongside …
items.body:
### Your Question

# Summary
This RFC proposes enabling DSpark speculative decoding support on Ascend NPU within the Vime framework. The change adapts the NPU batch-reordering logic to accommodate DSpark's speculative-decoding layout requirements, allowing DSpark to be launched alongside standard attention groups on Ascend hardware.

https://github.com/momo609/vime/tree/ascend

# Design
https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/issues/377

# Usage

DSpark is enabled through the standard vLLM speculative-config interface. The configuration is passed as a JSON string via --vllm-speculative-config, and the launch script is invoked with the usual RL-training arguments plus a set of vLLM-specific flags. The two essential fields for DSpark are method (set to "dspark") and model (pointing to the DSpark draft checkpoint). The optional fields control the number of speculative tokens, tensor-parallel size of the draft model, and where the updated draft weights are saved after training.
example: 
```
SPEC_CONFIG=$(printf '%s' \
  '{"method":"dspark",' \
  '"model":"{your path}/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7",' \
  '"num_speculative_tokens":7,' \
  '"draft_tensor_parallel_size":1}')

VLLM_ARGS=(
   --rollout-num-gpus-per-engine 4
   --vllm-weight-sync-mode native
   --vllm-enable-sleep-mode
   --vllm-gpu-memory-utilization 0.6
   --vllm-max-model-len 4096
   --vllm-speculative-config "$SPEC_CONFIG"
   --draft-save-hf {your path}/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7_after
)
```

# TEST
we have test Qwen3-4B with dspark on Ascend:

items.title: [CI/Build][Hardware][AMD] Rebuild the ROCm image on vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly
items.author: indianspeedster
items.summary: built everything from — ROCm 7.0.2, PyTorch, triton, flash-attention, aiter and vLLM all from source. AMD now publishes with that whole inference half already built, so this layers on it and adds only the training half, mirroring how layers on.
items.body:
## What

`docker/Dockerfile.rocm` built everything from `ubuntu:22.04` — ROCm 7.0.2, PyTorch, triton, flash-attention, aiter and vLLM all from source. AMD now publishes `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly` with that whole inference half already built, so this layers on it and adds only the training half, mirroring how `docker/Dockerfile` layers on `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly`.

**Result: 51.9 GB on disk / 12.7 GB compressed, down from 81.9 / 21.6**, and the build drops from hours to ~15 min (TransformerEngine is the only long compile).

Added on top of the base: TransformerEngine (`ROCm/TransformerEngine` v2_15_rocm, gfx950), apex, Megatron-LM plus the `docker/amd_patch/` patches, torch_memory_saver, rsync (the base omits it and `command_utils.rsync_simple` shells out to it), the vime requirements and vime itself, including the `int4_qat` HIP kernel the old image never built.

Dropped as now redundant: the ROCm/torch/triton/flash-attention/aiter/vLLM source builds, the cupy and xgrammar/tilelang/fastapi pins, and the TransformerEngine flash-attn `max_version` sed (2.8.3 is exactly TE 2.15's cap).

## Three things this base needs that the CUDA one does not

- **`VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=1`.** This vLLM gates the token-in-token-out endpoints behind an env var defaulting to off; older nightlies mounted them unconditionally. Without it every rollout request to `/inference/v1/generate` 404s. `docker/Dockerfile` will need this too once its base rolls forward.
- **`GPU_ARCHS`.** ROCm apex imports aiter, which resolves the live gfx arch at module import, so `megatron.training` cannot be imported without a visible GPU. Pinning the arch fixes the build-time codegen path; the runtime dispatch still needs a device, which is why the image's import check stops at `megatron.core`.
- **A tolerant vLLM patch apply.** See below.

## Patch handling vs. `docker/patch/latest/`

The ROCm nightly is cut from a different point on vLLM main than the CUDA base the patches are written against — ahead of it on some files, behind on others. So everything goes through `patch --fuzz=3` rather than `git apply`, and a single `.rej` sweep is what proves each hunk landed.

Four hunks or files do not fit. Each is dropped behind a check that **fails the build once the base converges**, so none of them can quietly outlive the drift that motivated it:

| Dropped | Why | Guard |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-Omni audio-encoder hunk in `vllm.patch` | Already upstream here, in a better form (TP sharding when the head count divides, `disable_tp` otherwise) | `grep -q 'disable_tp=self.disable_tp'` |
| `output_processor` delta-sampling-mask hunk (from #410) | Rewrites a block built on `SamplingMaskLists.merge`, which this base does not have. ROCm keeps emitting sampling masks only on finish | fails if `def merge` appears in `vllm/v1/outputs.py` |
| `vllm-pd-request-metrics.patch`, in full (from #410) | Patches `vllm/entrypoints/openai/engine/protocol.py`, a module this base splits across `generate/base/` and `serve/engine/`. Cost is per-request PD telemetry, which vime reads defensively in `observability/trace_utils.py` | fails if that path appears |
| `tests/` and `rust/` hunks | No target — site-packages ships neither tree | n/a |

`vllm-inflight-queue-diagnostics.patch` (from #410) applies in full.

`numpy` stays pinned to 1.x as in `docker/Dockerfile` — vime asserts it in `megatron_utils.initialize` — which costs the base's `cupy-rocm-7-0`, built against the numpy 2 ABI. Nothing in vime, vLLM, aiter or Megatron imports it.

## Test plan

Built and run on 8x MI350X. The image reports torch 2.12.0+git6bbd260 / hip 7.2.53211, vLLM 0.28.1rc1.dev516+g9ea8f3ffc, TransformerEngine 2.15.0+e7835ed.

The gating ROCm CI step reproduced locally against the built image, exactly as `.buildkite/pipeline-rocm.yaml` invokes it:

```
tests/test_qwen2.5_0.5B_fully_async_short.py   (4 GPU)
```

**Result: passes, exit 0.** `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff` = 0.0117 (step 0) and 0.0155 (step 1) against the 0.1 CI threshold; rollout-vs-ref logprobs agree at -0.29962 / -0.29944 and -0.45356 / -0.45456. `/inference/v1/generate` served 200 OK throughout at ~8.4k tok/s generation.

## Summary

Fixes #2388.

Keep caller-provided token IDs intact across Qwen-VL image turns. The active SGLang patches force the legacy multimodal loader, bypassing the original-ID side channel. For example, a previous response containing tokens `[350, 3140]` (" TCL") is re-tokenized as `[65231]`.

Remove that override from both active patch sets. The geo3k multi-turn example now sends unexpanded image placeholders to SGLang while retaining processor-expanded IDs for training, and appends generated IDs unchanged to both sequences. Environment observations use the current `Sample.append_response_tokens()` contract (`log_probs=None` for non-trainable tokens), which avoids the existing exception at the first observation.

Add ten CPU regression cases and register them in the regular CPU CI matrix. The fixture adds the repository root to its import path so direct script execution can import the example with CI's editable package install.

## Validation

- 25 targeted tests passed. On head `539b55dc986370733296629737f9a2cfd88aa332`, direct execution with `env -u PYTHONPATH .venv/bin/python tests/test_geo3k_vlm_multi_turn_tokens.py` also passed all ten cases.
- The ten new tests all fail on original main at the observation API mismatch. With only that prerequisite corrected, six image-token cases fail and four text-only controls pass.
- Both active patches apply to pinned SGLang `0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd`.
- Real Qwen3-VL-2B tokenizer/processor and native SGLang multimodal processing preserve all caller IDs after the fix for one and two images. The baseline loses one token in each case (94 vs. 95 and 166 vs. 167).
- Two-turn checks with real processors, including a new image in the second turn, produce expanded inference IDs identical to the training sequence; loss-mask/logprob lengths remain aligned.
- Black, isort, Ruff, `git diff --check`, and workflow regeneration passed.

Validation ran on CPU on the remote RTX 4090 host. The processor integration checks inject deterministic response IDs; model generation, HTTP serving, a rebuilt official container, and a full RL training run were not exercised. Existing images/environments need the updated SGLang patch to receive the loader fix.

items.title: [Bug] Qwen-VL patch bypasses SGLang token-ID preservation and breaks multi-turn TITO
items.author: dirtyDan0
items.summary: That argument therefore remains: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/baseprocessor.py#L952-L977 The caller IDs are still present in, but immediately decodes that list int…
items.body:
### Bug Description


Slime changes Qwen-VL from `load_mm_data()` to a direct `legacy_load_mm_data()` call:

https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/4c193f1f37509cca70f0e88807a9305b70f63f4e/docker/patch/latest/sglang.patch#L1248-L1260

This bypasses the code that preserves caller-provided token IDs.

In SGLang v0.5.15.post1, `load_mm_data()` first saves a `list[int]` prompt as `input_ids`, then
decodes the prompt for multimodal processing:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/base_processor.py#L785-L821

```python
input_ids = prompt if isinstance(prompt, list) else None
prompt = self._tokenizer.decode(prompt)
```

If `load_mm_data()` needs the legacy loader, it forwards the saved IDs through the separate
`input_ids=input_ids` argument:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/base_processor.py#L833-L864

The Slime patch calls `legacy_load_mm_data(prompt=input_text, ...)` directly and does not pass its
separate `input_ids` argument. That argument therefore remains `None`:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/base_processor.py#L952-L977

The caller IDs are still present in `prompt`, but `legacy_load_mm_data()` immediately decodes that
list into text. It later returns the decoded/reconstructed text together with `input_ids=None`:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/base_processor.py#L1065-L1070

For raw images, `process_and_combine_mm_data()` then invokes the HF processor on that text and takes
the processor's newly generated `ret["input_ids"]`:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/base_processor.py#L1188-L1204

SGLang's protection against this retokenization requires `base_output.input_ids is not None`:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/base_processor.py#L1328-L1383

The caller must send pre-expansion rollout IDs: one image placeholder per image, together with the
exact token IDs returned by earlier generation turns. SGLang owns image-placeholder expansion for
its forward pass. The processor-expanded sequence can be retained separately for training.

Because the Slime patch leaves that field as `None`, the protection branch can never run. The raw
image path therefore always follows:

```text
caller input_ids
  -> decode to text
  -> HF processor
  -> newly tokenized input_ids
```

This means retokenization is executed for every affected request. The resulting IDs do not
necessarily differ on every request: canonical token sequences may round-trip unchanged. For a
non-canonical sequence, `encode(decode(input_ids))` can differ from the caller's IDs, causing token
drift.

SGLang upstream added the preservation path specifically for this problem in
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/26555

The fix is already present in the SGLang revision pinned by Slime, but the Slime patch bypasses it.


### Steps to Reproduce


Run this CPU-only comparison in an SGLang v0.5.15.post1 source environment with the
`Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` tokenizer. The first response ends with `<|im_end|>` and contains the valid
but non-canonical IDs `[479, 3770]` (`["Ġtr", "uly"]`) before it. Those two IDs decode to
`" truly"` and re-tokenize as the single ID `[9149]` (`["Ġtruly"]`). No SGLang source change or
model weights are required.

```python
import asyncio
from difflib import SequenceMatcher

from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoProcessor

from sglang.srt.managers.schedule_batch import MultimodalInputFormat
from sglang.srt.multimodal.processors.base_processor import MultimodalSpecialTokens
from sglang.srt.multimodal.processors.qwen_vl import QwenVLImageProcessor
from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs


async def main():
    model_name = "Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B"
    hf_processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_name)
    tokenizer = hf_processor.tokenizer
    processor = QwenVLImageProcessor(
        AutoConfig.from_pretrained(model_name),
        ServerArgs(model_path=model_name),
        hf_processor,
        "default",
        skip_mm_pool=True,
    )
    # Turn 1 prompt, including one image placeholder.
    prompt_ids = tokenizer.encode(
        "<|im_start|>user\nWhat is shown?"
        "<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|im_end|>\n"
        "<|im_start|>assistant\n",
        add_special_tokens=False,
    )

    # Turn 1 response exactly as generated by SGLang, including the assistant
    # turn terminator. Each ID is annotated with its token and decoded text:
    response_ids = [
        479,     # token "Ġtr", decoded fragment " tr"
        3770,    # token "uly", decoded fragment "uly"
        248046,  # token "<|im_end|>", decoded assistant-turn terminator
    ]

    # Turn 2 starts after the complete response above.
    next_prompt_ids = tokenizer.encode(
        "\n<|im_start|>user\nExplain your answer.<|im_end|>\n"
        "<|im_start|>assistant\n",
        add_special_tokens=False,
    )
    accumulated_ids = prompt_ids + response_ids + next_prompt_ids

    tokens = MultimodalSpecialTokens(
        image_token="<|image_pad|>",
        image_token_id=tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("<|image_pad|>"),
    )
    tokens.parse_regex()
    # Valid preprocessed input keeps this loader comparison CPU-only.
    image_data = [{"format": MultimodalInputFormat.PROCESSOR_OUTPUT}]
    try:
        normal = await processor.load_mm_data(
            prompt=accumulated_ids,
            multimodal_tokens=tokens,
            image_data=image_data,
        )
        legacy = await processor.legacy_load_mm_data(
            prompt=accumulated_ids,
            multimodal_tokens=tokens,
            image_data=image_data,
        )
        _, normal_ids, _ = processor.process_and_combine_mm_data(normal, tokens)
        _, legacy_ids, _ = processor.process_and_combine_mm_data(legacy, tokens)
    finally:
        processor.io_executor.shutdown()
        processor.cpu_executor.shutdown()

    normal_ids = normal_ids.tolist()
    legacy_ids = legacy_ids.tolist()
    print("response tokens:")
    for index, token_id in enumerate(response_ids):
        print(
            f"  {index}: id={token_id}, "
            f"token={tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(token_id)!r}, "
            f"text={tokenizer.decode([token_id])!r}"
        )
    print("load_mm_data preserved caller IDs:", normal.input_ids == accumulated_ids)
    print("legacy_load_mm_data input_ids:", legacy.input_ids)
    print("normal final IDs preserved caller IDs:", normal_ids == accumulated_ids)
    print(
        "legacy decoded text matches caller:",
        legacy.input_text == tokenizer.decode(accumulated_ids),
    )

    differences = []
    for tag, caller_start, caller_end, legacy_start, legacy_end in SequenceMatcher(
        a=accumulated_ids, b=legacy_ids, autojunk=False
    ).get_opcodes():
        if tag == "equal":
            continue
        caller_span = accumulated_ids[caller_start:caller_end]
        legacy_span = legacy_ids[legacy_start:legacy_end]
        differences.append((tag, caller_span, legacy_span))
        print(f"{tag}:")
        print(
            f"  caller/load_mm_data[{caller_start}:{caller_end}]",
            list(zip(caller_span, tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(caller_span))),
        )
        print(
            f"  legacy retokenized[{legacy_start}:{legacy_end}]",
            list(zip(legacy_span, tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(legacy_span))),
        )

    assert normal.input_ids == accumulated_ids
    assert legacy.input_ids is None
    assert normal_ids == accumulated_ids
    # Expected: the prior response's two IDs become one ID after retokenization.
    assert differences == [("replace", [479, 3770], [9149])]


asyncio.run(main())
```

Expected output:

```text
response tokens:
  0: id=479, token='Ġtr', text=' tr'
  1: id=3770, token='uly', text='uly'
  2: id=248046, token='<|im_end|>', text='<|im_end|>'
load_mm_data preserved caller IDs: True
legacy_load_mm_data input_ids: None
normal final IDs preserved caller IDs: True
legacy decoded text matches caller: True
replace:
  caller/load_mm_data[14:16] [(479, 'Ġtr'), (3770, 'uly')]
  legacy retokenized[14:15] [(9149, 'Ġtruly')]
```

This matches the Slime patch exactly: it calls `legacy_load_mm_data(prompt=input_text, ...)` without
`input_ids=input_text`, so the original IDs are not retained for the anti-retokenization branch.

The original Qwen3-VL diagnosis captured the same pattern in three real multi-turn failures:

```text
[350, 3140] ["ĠT", "CL"]       -> [65231] ["ĠTCL"]
[1760, 529] ["Ġcount", "ert"] -> [60110] ["Ġcountert"]
[1841, 424] ["Ġsign", "age"]  -> [79080] ["Ġsignage"]
```

### Expected Behavior

For pre-tokenized image requests, the caller should send pre-expansion rollout IDs with one image
placeholder per image. SGLang should preserve every caller-provided non-image ID, including prior
response IDs, and expand the image placeholder for its forward pass.


### Actual Behavior

The Slime patch loses the original-ID side channel. SGLang decodes the caller IDs and adopts the HF
processor's re-tokenized IDs, even though `SGLANG_MM_AVOID_RETOKENIZE` is enabled by default.

### Environment

- slime commit: `4c193f1f37509cca70f0e88807a9305b70f63f4e`
- SGLang version: v0.5.15.post1
- OS: Linux

### Logs

```shell

```

### Additional Context

## Suggested Fix

Remove the Qwen-VL `load_mm_data()` to `legacy_load_mm_data()` override from the active Slime SGLang
patches. `load_mm_data()` already falls back to `legacy_load_mm_data()` when needed while preserving
the original IDs through `input_ids=input_ids`.

The multi-turn VLM rollout should also keep pre-expansion rollout IDs separately from the
processor-expanded training IDs and send the rollout IDs to SGLang. The current recipe writes
processor output directly into `sample.tokens` and later sends that same sequence as `input_ids`:

https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/4c193f1f37509cca70f0e88807a9305b70f63f4e/examples/geo3k_vlm_multi_turn/rollout.py#L154-L179

https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/4c193f1f37509cca70f0e88807a9305b70f63f4e/examples/geo3k_vlm_multi_turn/rollout.py#L192-L200


### Pre-submission Checklist

- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and understand the collaboration scope.
- [x] I have read the [documentation](https://thudm.github.io/slime/) and my issue is not addressed there.
- [x] I have searched for [existing issues](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/issues) and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I have provided a minimal, reproducible example.

items.body:
## Summary

Add the serving-side patches required by disk-backed full and delta weight synchronization on Ascend:

- append the vLLM disk checkpoint loader and its regression coverage to `docker/npu_patch/vllm.patch`
- append `NPUWorker.pull_weights()` to `docker/npu_patch/vllm-ascend.patch`

The PR is based directly on the current `vllm-project/vime:ascend` branch and changes only these two patch files.

## Dependency

Depends on #413 for the VIME-side disk full/delta weight synchronization flow and its pinned vLLM/vLLM-Ascend revisions. After #413 merges, this branch can be rebased onto the updated `ascend` branch and merged directly.

## Validation

Validated on Ascend NPUs 8-15 with Qwen3-4B, disk transport, `num_rollout=10`, rollout batch size 4, two samples per prompt, and response length 256. The table excludes the final v10 update because it overlaps Ray/vLLM job teardown; it compares the initial sync and stable v1-v9 updates.

| Stage | Delta ratio | Delta wire | Delta update | Delta E2E | Full ratio | Full checkpoint | Full update | Full E2E |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Initial sync | - | - | 5.64s | 34.05s | - | - | 6.13s | 48.41s |
| v1 | 0.56% | 0.13 GB | 10.19s | 28.45s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 6.59s | 31.09s |
| v2 | 0.63% | 0.14 GB | 4.67s | 21.66s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 6.41s | 30.36s |
| v3 | 0.70% | 0.15 GB | 4.24s | 20.49s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 7.26s | 31.12s |
| v4 | 0.60% | 0.13 GB | 4.98s | 28.05s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 5.83s | 26.13s |
| v5 | 0.84% | 0.17 GB | 4.17s | 20.98s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 6.91s | 25.66s |
| v6 | 0.63% | 0.14 GB | 4.23s | 20.89s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 6.12s | 26.96s |
| v7 | 0.61% | 0.13 GB | 4.34s | 21.32s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 6.59s | 28.42s |
| v8 | 0.58% | 0.13 GB | 4.16s | 21.11s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 6.79s | 29.80s |
| v9 | 0.77% | 0.16 GB | 4.30s | 21.54s | 100% | 7.49 GiB | 6.38s | 29.86s |
| v1-v9 mean | 0.66% | ~0.14 GB | **5.03s** | - | 100% | 7.49 GiB | **6.54s** | - |
| 10 rollout steps | - | - | - | **238.55s** | - | - | - | **307.81s** |

E2E uses `perf/step_time` and covers rollout, training wait, training, and the update attributed to the step. Delta transfers about 0.66% of the model on average, but vLLM still reloads a reconstructed 7.49 GiB safetensors checkpoint on this NPU path. 


### Qwen3-0.6B disk delta validation

Added `tests/test_delta_disk_weight_update.py` to run XOR and overwrite sequentially with Qwen3-0.6B. Each encoding runs two rollout/training rounds on four Ascend devices (one training, three rollout), with graph mode enabled. The test validates delta metadata and final recovered tensor checksums.

python3 tests/test_delta_disk_weight_update.py

...
Disk delta validation passed: {'encoding': 'xor', 'rollout_rounds': 2, 'local_version': '000002', 'checked_tensors': 240}

items.title: [Question] Would an adaptive in-reward KL controller fit Slime's PPO/RLHF scope?
items.author: hkxxxxx
items.summary: The default behavior would remain fixed-coefficient and unchanged. This would run alongside PPO clipping; it would not modify epsclip or the PPO ratio objective.
items.body:
### Your Question

## Question

Would an opt-in adaptive in-reward KL controller for PPO-style reference-policy training fit Slime's current scope for general-purpose RL optimizations?

## Proposal

The proposal is deliberately limited to the existing PPO/RLHF-style reward-side KL path:

observed reference KL -> update beta -> next-batch reward shaping
r'_t = task_reward_t - beta * KL_t

The controller would adapt the existing --kl-coef between batches toward a target KL, with bounded updates, a configurable horizon, checkpointed state, and metrics for observed KL, target KL, coefficient, and update status. The default behavior would remain fixed-coefficient and unchanged.

This would run alongside PPO clipping; it would not modify eps_clip or the PPO ratio objective.

## Scope boundary

This is not a proposal to change the current GRPO reward semantics. I understand the maintainer direction in #399: GRPO should prefer kl_loss unless experiments show that reward-side KL is beneficial. The first implementation would target PPO-style training only, where reward-side KL is already part of the existing path.

Would a focused implementation with unit tests and a reproducible training benchmark be considered an in-scope general-purpose RL optimization? If so, I would be happy to prepare a small PR rather than a broad abstraction proposal.

### What I've Tried

I checked the current Slime implementation and related discussions:

- #397 identified that GRPO's non-zero --kl-coef was effectively ignored.
- #399 proposed applying KL to GRPO rewards, but the maintainer discussion preferred kl_loss for GRPO unless supported by experiments.
- #1247 made a similar GRPO reward-side change and was closed without being merged.
- In the current PPO path, --kl-coef is applied during token-level reward construction before GAE.
- In verl's implementation, AdaptiveKLController updates the coefficient from the batch KL toward a target KL. The implementation cites Ziegler et al.'s RLHF work (arXiv:1909.08593).

I have intentionally not included GRPO, TTTD, OPD, standalone kl_loss_coef, or evaluation/rollback orchestration in this proposal. Those have different semantics and should be considered separately.

### Environment (if relevant)

This is an algorithm/API-scope question rather than a runtime bug. No specific hardware or environment is required at this stage.

### Additional Context

Related discussion: Human-Agent-Society/reef#466.

The goal is to clarify ownership and scope before writing code. Slime would own the training-side controller; any held-out evaluation or publish/pause/rollback policy would remain outside this proposed Slime change.

### Pre-submission Checklist

- [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and understand the collaboration scope.
- [x] I have read the [documentation](https://thudm.github.io/slime/) and [FAQ](https://thudm.github.io/slime/en/get_started/qa.html) and my question is not answered there.
- [x] I have searched for [existing issues](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/issues) and my question has not been asked before.

items.title: fix(ascend): harden disk delta checkpoint handling
items.author: wangx700
items.summary: Hardens disk-delta checkpoint handling for the Ascend disk weight-sync path, on top of the NPU platformization work in #413: - Deterministic shard discovery (sorted ) and fail-fast on empty checkpoint dirs - Strict safetensors header validation: truncation che…
items.body:
## What

Hardens disk-delta checkpoint handling for the Ascend disk weight-sync path, on top of the NPU platformization work in #413:

**`vime/utils/disk_delta.py`**
- Deterministic shard discovery (sorted `*.safetensors`) and fail-fast `FileNotFoundError` on empty checkpoint dirs
- Strict safetensors header validation: truncation checks on the length prefix and header bytes, header length bounded by file size, JSON-object header check
- Per-tensor `data_offsets` bounds checking (`0 <= begin <= end <= data_size`) and truncated-read detection in the tensor reader - corrupted or partially written checkpoints now raise a descriptive `RuntimeError` instead of silently materializing wrong weights

**`vime/backends/megatron_utils/update_weight/update_weight_from_disk_delta.py`**
- Pinned host-buffer pool extracted into `_make_pinned_pool`, bounded to 8 GiB total pinned allocation, with graceful fallback to pageable `.cpu()` copies
- Buffer ownership hardened: pinned buffers are always returned to the pool via `try/finally`, both when a pool worker fails and when task submission is interrupted (no pinned-memory leak / pool starvation on transient errors)

## Why

Mirrors the checkpoint hardening from #422 (bound disk delta buffers and validate checkpoints) onto the #413 platformization base, where the disk delta path runs on shared filesystems that can surface truncated or partially committed checkpoint files.

## Notes
- Stacked on #413: the diff vs `ascend` includes #413's commits until that PR merges.
- Scope is intentionally minimal - only the two hardening-related files change.

## Test plan
- [ ] `pytest tests/unit` (CPU)
- [ ] 910 end-to-end smoke: `--update-weight-mode delta --update-weight-transport disk` (in progress on the NPU environment)

items.title: [Bug] Broadcasting full rollout_routed_experts data to every Megatron training rank will cause host OOM
items.author: JayPritchet
items.summary: Each actor then locally performs padding, concatenation, CP slicing, and optionally TP slicing through. For large MoE training batches, this creates a large host-memory peak at the beginning of.
items.body: ### Bug Description When `--use-rollout-routing-replay` is enabled, the complete DP-local `rollout_routed_experts` payload is transferred to every Megatron training actor in the same DP group. Each actor then locally performs padding, concatenation, CP slicing, and optionally TP slicing through `prepare_routed_experts_for_routing_replay()`. For large MoE training batches, this creates a large host-memory peak at the beginning of `MegatronTrainRayActor.train`. Under some configurations, the peak causes host OOM. `rollout_routed_experts` has an approximate shape of: ```text [num_tokens, num_moe_layers, router_topk] ``` Its size therefore grows with all of the following: - rollout batch size; - sequence length; - number of MoE layers; - router top-k. Unlike token-level scalar fields such as log probabilities, rollout_routed_experts stores multiple expert IDs for every token and every MoE layer. ## example In my situation, I train glm-4.7-flash (num_moe_layers=47, router_topk=4) with this config : - `--use-rollout-routing-replay` - rollout batch size: 96 - group size: 16 - max response len: 64k - cp=2 tp=4 I was trainning using fully async on 2 node each with 8*H800 and 1.6TB Memory, 1node for rollout and 1 node for training. The average resp len is about 32k, so the total size of rollout data would be: ``` 96 prompts × 16 samples per prompt × 32,768 tokens × 47 MoE layers × 4 experts per token × 4 bytes per int32 ≈ 35.25 GiB ``` If all 8 Megatron training actors receive and hold their own copy of this payload, the aggregate host-memory consumption can reach approximately: 35.25 GiB × 8 actors ≈ 282 GiB. This is only the routed-experts preparation overhead. It is in addition to the Ray Object Store payload, model processes, training data, pinned routing replay buffers, and other runtime memory. As a result, this memory spike can easily lead to host OOM. The following graph shows the corresponding USS spike at the beginning of MegatronTrainRayActor.train: ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Train `glm-4.7-flash` with `--use-rollout-routing-replay` enabled. 2. Use a fully async setup with: * 1 node (8× H800) for rollout * 1 node (8× H800) for Megatron training * rollout batch size: `96` * group size: `16` * max response length: `64k` * average response length: ~`32k` * CP: `2` * TP: `4` 3. Start training and monitor host memory usage at the beginning of `MegatronTrainRayActor.train`. ### Expected Behavior The training is heathy and will not encouter host OOM. ### Actual Behavior The training is heathy for a few steps, then it encouters an OOM. ### Environment - slime version: 0.3.2 - Python version: 3.12 - PyTorch version: 2.11.0+cu129 - CUDA/ROCm version: 13.0 - GPU type and count: 2*8 H800 - OS: Ubuntu - SGLang version (if relevant): - Megatron-LM version (if relevant): ### Logs ```shell ``` ### Additional Context _No response_ ### Pre-submission Checklist - [x] I have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and understand the collaboration scope. - [x] I have read the [documentation](https://thudm.github.io/slime/) and my issue is not addressed there. - [x] I have searched for [existing issues](https://github.com/THUDM/slime/issues) and this is not a duplicate. - [x] I have provided a minimal, reproducible example.

items.title: feat: add fused Triton log-probability backend for Megatron
items.author: YolandaLyj
items.summary: This substantially increases peak GPU memory for long packed sequences and can cause OOMs. A Qwen3.5-4B fixed-rollout acceptance matrix completed all eight target TP/SP/CP/PP topologies, including PP=2 with four microbatches.
items.body:
## Problem

The Megatron policy and reference log-probability paths materialize
`[tokens, vocab_per_tp_rank]` logits. This substantially increases peak GPU
memory for long packed sequences and can cause OOMs.

## Changes

- Add an opt-in fused Triton backend with `--log-probs-backend triton`.
- Keep the existing PyTorch path as the default with
  `--log-probs-backend torch`.
- Support Megatron policy/reference computation with TP, SP, CP, and
  non-interleaved PP.
- Match the existing BF16 output-boundary behavior.
- Vendor the Apache-2.0 kernel from verl commit
  `4905d0cf4ebc7297231e15efa4cf837163efca45`, retaining its license and NOTICE attribution.

## Validation

Focused tests on 2 × H200, using PyTorch 2.11.0+cu129, Triton 3.6.0, and
Megatron Core 0.16.0rc0:

```text
python tests/test_triton_log_probs.py
10 passed

python -m pytest -q \
  tests/test_triton_log_probs_integration.py \
  tests/test_megatron_argument_validation.py
29 passed
```

The tests cover:

- Log-probability and entropy forward/backward parity.
- TP and SP communication and gradient parity.
- CP token alignment and empty-rank backward.
- PP-stage integration and backend configuration validation.

A Qwen3.5-4B fixed-rollout acceptance matrix completed all eight target
TP/SP/CP/PP topologies, including PP=2 with four microbatches. Compared with
the standard PyTorch path:

- Actor/reference log-probability max absolute difference: `3.815e-6`
- Entropy max absolute difference: `1.087e-4`
- Actor loss max absolute difference: `1.192e-7`
- Global gradient-norm max relative difference: `1.399e-3`
- Peak allocated GPU memory reduction: `23.05%–54.14%`

Profiler traces did not contain a materialized full
`[tokens, vocab_per_tp_rank]` logits tensor.

## Limitations

The Triton backend currently supports the Megatron actor policy/reference
paths with BF16 CUDA tensors. It does not support non-policy losses, rollout
top-p replay, MTP, virtual pipeline parallelism, or output layers with bias.

items.author: 0z5a
items.summary: Reject malformed sampled-token log probabilities before appending generated data or calculating rewards. Previously, two token IDs with one probability could be padded with zero and accepted as training data.
items.body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/vllm-project/vime/pull/426/files).

items.title: fix: restore actor weights before initial rollout sync
items.author: tengeel
items.summary: Without, initialization leaves the last auxiliary checkpoint active. Both training entry points synchronize rollout weights before the first training step, so distributed or disk-based synchronization can publish auxiliary weights instead of the resumed actor…
items.body:
## Problem

`MegatronTrainRayActor.init()` backs up the actor and then loads reference, teacher, or old-actor checkpoints into the same model.

Without `--offload-train`, initialization leaves the last auxiliary checkpoint active. Both training entry points synchronize rollout weights before the first training step, so distributed or disk-based synchronization can publish auxiliary weights instead of the resumed actor.

For one resumed run:

| | rollout logprob | reference logprob | actor logprob |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Before | -0.1106 | -0.1111 | -0.1471 |
| After | -0.1088 | -0.1421 | -0.1095 |

Before the fix, rollout weights match the reference. After the fix, they match the resumed actor.

## Fix

- Restore the actor after loading auxiliary checkpoints.
- Reject rollout weight synchronization when the actor is not active.

## Tests

```bash
python tests/test_actor_first_weight_update.py -q
```

```text
5 passed
```

The tests cover reference, teacher, and old-actor restoration, the already-active case, and rejection of a non-actor weight update.

Fixes #1695

items.title: feat(modelexpress): add S3 delta weight update backend
items.author: nv-hwoo
items.summary: Add ModelExpress as a Vime weight-update backend for canonical S3 delta synchronization, with the implementation owned by the ModelExpress SDK. [Discussion: <!-- readthedocs-1185709 --> ### Documentation build overview > 📚 📁 Comparing 8095aafdbba2622627fbc3]
items.body:
## Summary

Add ModelExpress as a Vime weight-update backend for canonical S3 delta synchronization, with the implementation owned by the ModelExpress SDK.

**This PR depends on [ai-dynamo/modelexpress#846](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/modelexpress/pull/846).** Merge/use that MX change first: Vime now re-exports `UpdateWeightFromModelExpress` from `modelexpress_rl.train.frameworks.vime.modelexpress`, so a ModelExpress build containing that adapter is required.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T["Vime Megatron trainer"] --> A["MX-owned Vime adapter"]
    A -->|"delta / full HF payloads"| S3["S3-compatible storage"]
    A -->|"version lifecycle"| C["ModelExpress catalog"]
    C --> V["Native vLLM ModelExpress WTE"]
    S3 --> V
```

## What changed

| Owner | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| This Vime PR | `--update-weight-transport modelexpress`, JSON configuration/validation, lazy adapter re-export, native vLLM backend selection, and wiring tests |
| Dependent MX PR | Canonical HF export/chunk ownership, v0 registration, delta/full-checkpoint publication, rollout-update lifecycle, metrics, and implementation tests |

The MX adapter:

- Creates a catalog-only READY v0 and captures the initial seed as the delta baseline; no v0 files are uploaded.
- Publishes XOR delta payloads by default and full HF checkpoints at `full_hf_checkpoint_interval`.
- Pauses generation, flushes cache, starts the update, installs the exact version, finishes the update, and resumes generation.
- Preserves tied-embedding handling and forwards `refit_checkpoint_max_size_gb` to the receiver.
- Reports delta density, published bytes, staging/publication time, and rollout-update time.

Other Vime transports do not require ModelExpress. The adapter is imported only when the ModelExpress transport is selected.

## Configuration

```bash
--update-weight-transport modelexpress \
--modelexpress-config '{
  "model_name": "policy",
  "server_url": "modelexpress:8101",
  "initial_base_version_id": "policy-v0",
  "seed_checkpoint_path": "/models/policy",
  "refit_checkpoint_dir": "/tmp/mx-refit",
  "refit_checkpoint_max_size_gb": 200,
  "object_storage_uri_prefix": "s3://weight-updates/policy",
  "object_storage_endpoint_url": "http://minio:9000",
  "object_storage_region_name": "us-east-1",
  "full_hf_checkpoint_interval": 10
}'
```

This example uses MinIO. For AWS S3, omit `object_storage_endpoint_url` and use the bucket's region and normal AWS credential configuration. The receiver cache quota is in decimal GB; omission retains the MX default and `null` disables the quota.

## Scope

S3-compatible storage with canonical delta payloads and periodic full HF checkpoints. ModelExpress P2P transfer and Dynamo-specific external rollout integration are outside this PR. vLLM uses its native `modelexpress` weight-transfer backend.

## Testing

- `PYTHONPATH=. python -m pytest -q -o addopts= tests/test_megatron_argument_validation.py tests/test_update_weight_factory.py tests/test_modelexpress_vllm.py` — **33 passed**.
- MX adapter behavior and optional-import tests — **23 passed** in the dependent MX PR.
- `git diff --check` — passed in both repositories.

The updater's implementation tests now live in MX; Vime keeps argument validation, lazy factory/re-export, and vLLM backend-selection coverage.

## E2E Validation

| Setting | Validated configuration |
|---|---|
| Model | Qwen3-30B-A3B, BF16 |
| Trainer | 4 B200 GPUs; TP2 / PP2 / EP2 / ETP1 / CP1 |
| Rollout | 4 B200 GPUs; TP4, separate node |
| Workload | GSM8K/math; 24 rollouts; rollout batch 4 × 8; global batch 32 |
| Storage | AWS S3 |
| Full HF checkpoint interval | N=10: v10 and v20 |
| Receiver checkpoint-cache quota | 200 decimal GB |
| vLLM integration | Native ModelExpress WTE, verified with `VLLM_PLUGINS=""` |

| Payload | Updates | Count | Mean update time | Median | Min–max |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Delta payload | v1–v9, v11–v19, v21–v24 | 22 | 54.7 s | 49.3 s | 43.7–103.2 s |
| Full HF checkpoint | v10, v20 | 2 | 543.2 s | 543.2 s | 538.5–547.9 s |

Timing covers the entire native Vime `update_weights` call: export, S3 publication, receiver preparation/install, and completion—not network transfer alone. v0 bootstrap is excluded. Update 24's timer has 0.1-second precision.

- All **24 updates installed on all four rollout TP workers**.
- All **25 catalog records**, including v0, were READY with the expected formats and lineage; **no v0 payload upload**.
- Final receiver state was READY; four post-update generation checks returned the expected answers with finite, aligned token log probabilities.
- Trainer exited naturally with code 0; successful-attempt pods had zero restarts.
- Both pods verified the SDK-owned updater/re-export and native vLLM MX registration. No framework implementation changes were needed during GPU validation.
